Mr. W. E. KNOWLES (Moosejaw) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, to amend the Criminal Code.
/

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Explain.

The purpose of this Bill is to make it an offence for a manufacturer, selling goods to a wholesaler, to enhance or dictate in any way, by agreement or contract, the price at which the goods shall be sold. If the Bill is favourably considered by the House, the result in my opinion will be an immediate reduction of from 5 per cent to 10 per cent in the cost of many of the foodstuffs we consume. I have in my hand quite a number of these price-maintenance agreements, commencing with the E. B. Eddy Company, which the wholesale men are compelled to sign. These agreements dictate and bind in the most ridiculous and heartless way the wholesaler as to the price and conditions under which he shall sell the goods he has purchased. The object of this Bill is to prevent the continuance of that condition, and to leave the wholesaler or retailer, when he has purchased the goods, free to call them his own, and sell them for what he pleases.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. W. E. KNOWLES (Moosejaw) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 22, to amend the Grain Act.
Explain.

The Dominion Government has now gone intp the elevator business, having elevators at Moosejaw, Saskatoon, Calgary and Vancouver. The business is carried on between the Government and the farmers; the Government is also an employer of labour. I am seeking legislation to the effect that any claims against the Government shall be adjusted in the ordinary courts of the province, and also that the Workmen's Compensation Act shall apply to these Dominion Government employees just as it applies to the employees ,of any ordinary elevator company. The present system of having the claims brought before the Exchequer Court is very inconvenient and expensive, and the object of this Bill is to bring His Majesty into the same relation to his employees as is the ordinary subject who is engaged in this business.

speechtext: I have just received a letter from the parish priest of Port Daniel East, the Rev. J. Philippe Oyr, in which he calls attention to the fact that one of his parishioners, a young man named Joseph Doiron, has enlisted, leaving at home a wife and six young children, the eldest of whom is ten years, and the youngest nine months. His wife receives only $20 a month separation allowance. The parish priest wants to know if anything can be done to relieve this woman, either under the law as it stands,, or from the Patriotic Fund.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has the soldier assigned say part of his pay to his wife?
According to this letter, all she gets is the separation allowance of $20 a month.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps it would be worth while finding out whether she receives any assigned pay.

In the meantime, if she
is not receiving it, will this woman have

to be content with $20 a month? The right hon. gentleman will understand that if he wants to stimulate recruiting he will have to be a little more generous than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not quite clear at the moment whether there is any power to insist on a soldier assigning part of his pay to his family. I understand, however, that the Patriotic Fund makes provision in cases such as my hon. friend has mentioned.

I would ask the hon. member for Bonaventure if that woman has applied to the Patriotic Fund at Riviere du Loup. If she belongs to the district from Montmagny down to Gaspe, and would apply to the branch of the Patriotic Fund at Rivdere du Loup, of which I am president, she would receive $50 a month from the Patriotic Fund.

I understand that those
along the coast of my constituency would come under the Restigouche branch of the Patriotic Fund, with headquarters at Camp-bellton. This soldier is named Joseph Doiron. His number is 889720. He enrolled on February 23, 1916, with the 189th Battalion at New Carlisle. He has since been transferred to the 22nd Battalion, which is now at the front. His wife's name is Elizabeth Langlois, and she has six children. These particulars are given in a letter I have received from the parish priest at Port Daniel East.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would appear that if pay were assigned and if the ordinary allowance were made from the Patriotic Fund, this woman would be receiving something over $50 a month, as my hon. friend says she is already receiving $20 a month separation allowance.
I have some recollection that an order in council was passed, empowering us to deal with cases where a soldier at the front refuses to assign his pay.
I am informed by the deputy minister that there is an order in council which provides that if a man is married and has a family, one-half of his pay will, on application, be retained and paid over to his family while the man is serving at the front. Perhaps the reason that has not been done in this case is that the woman has not brought the matter to the attention of the department. Will my hon. friend' say whether that has been done or not?

On reading the letter
a second time, I see that it says the only
25i
amounts she has received is the separation allowance. I will hand the letter to the right hon. gentleman or to the Minister of Militia so that the case may be investigated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the matter
were brought to the attention of the proper officers of the department, and if the matter were also brought to the attention . of the Patriotic Fund, it is perfectly obvious that the family in question would be receiving something over fifty dollars per month, instead of twenty dollars per month. That really would be a more effective way of dealing with the matter than bringing it to my attention in the House of Commons, because I never heard of it until my hon. friend mentioned it.
Would the Prime Minister say as a matter of information if a soldier's wife who has six children dependent upon her receives the same separation allowance as the soldier's wife who has no children?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand
that, so far as the separation allowance is concerned, no distinction is drawn, but. so far as the Patriotic Fund is concerned, there is a distinction.

I would suggest the desirability of having printed in short form for distribution amongst the member's the rules regarding separation allowance. I put a question on the Order Paper to which I yesterday received a lengthy answer intimating that certain orders in council had been passed at different times; but it was impossible to gather any information from that answer without looking up the orders in council. It would facilitate matters if the department would have printed for members of this House a sucoinct statement of conditions in regard to separation allowances.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's suggestion is a very good one. I understand he does not want the printing of the orders in council, but the printing of their purport. The deputy minister informs me that the orders in council are being printed now, but it might be more convenient if the purport of them in simpler form were printed and distributed. The deputy minister informs me now that what I have just mentioned is also being done.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia another

matter similar to the one which I brought up last night. I received this morning a letter in regard to a case affected by the order in council that I mentioned. A civil engineer, who sacrificed a valuable business to enlist, entered an Edmonton battalion as a lieutenant on July 3, 1915. He was promoted to be a captain in December, 1915. He was wounded at Pozieres on September 13, 1916. He had a dependent and invalid mother and a young child; he had no wife. His sister kept the child and took care of the mother, receiving a captain's separation allowance of $40 per month up to the passing of this order in council, and since that time she has been receiving $12 per month only on account of the child. The writer says:
"My brother, Captain 

, has offered
without hesitation his life and poss ..ssions and no doubt the country will deal generously with him in return."
I think it is hardly generosity to cut down the captain's separation allowance to an allowance of $12 per month under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The large number of combinations that can occur in respect to separation allowance and similar matters is surprising. We are trying to consolidate them and the regulations are being printed , not only in respect to separation allowance but in respect to other things. I am to-day having certain other regulations printed which I purpose! having distributed amongst the members, in respect to requests for leave, which come under different headings and are being continually changed. Improvements are being made from time to time, and I hope that in time all these cases will be covered. That is all I can say today about the matter.

London, June 5th, 1916.
Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
Your cable 24th ultimo. Have communication from War Office covering letters recently-received from Commander in Chief Armies in France, who reports efficiency Ross rifle thoroughly tested by actual fighting in field, that he has again consulted General Officer Commanding Second Army in case fresh points have come to light during recent heavy fighting by Canadians near Ypres. Latter states his experience working Ross rifle during lr*st fight has only confirmed his opinilon that Canadians in Third Division have lost confidence in their rifle, and he recommends that rifles this Division be exchanged. Sir Douglas Haig remarks that although reports from Second Division not to same effect he is of opinion Lee-Enfleld rifle should be issued to all three divisions Canadian Corps. At my Council agree with this opinion and have approved his proposal to exchange rifles second and third divisions for Lee-Enfield pattern and steps will be taken forthwith effect exchange. Army Council hope be able utilize Ross rifles released from France, also those in possess'on Canadian troops England, for other purposes connected with war. They would be glad if steps could be taken stop any more R" ss rifles being brought to England, it being understood they thereby make themselves responsible (for supplying necessary rifles to Canadian troops on arrival here, and they see no reason to doubt being able do this. Army Council add should Canadian Govern-mentj be desirous undertaking manufacture! rifle of different patterns suitable for use during present war, in their opinion rifle made same pattern as now produced in United States for British army, which is on lines Lee-Enfleld, Mark III, embodying improvements, probably best one to adopt. Mailing copies correspondence. War Office wishes this matter regarded as secret until July 15th.
Perley.
Between 8th June and 5th July, the general commanding the forces in France, Sir Douglas Haig, had been asked by the authorities in England to make a report upon this rifle. The object was to put them in a position to give a satisfactory answer to the Canadian Government. I think that any hon. gentleman who reads the correspondence will come to the conclusion that this was the object. A report was made by Sir Douglas Haig, and evidently this must have been in the hands of the High Commissioner before he sent his communication to the Prime Minister.
This report is not very lengthy, and I purpose reading it. It is addressed to the Secretary of the War Office, London, and is as follows:
General Headquarters
British Army in the Field,
28th May, 1916.
Sir.-I have the honour to inform you that I have satisfied myself, after extensive inquiries carried out throughout the Canadian corps, that,

as a service rifle, the Ross is less trustworthy than the Lee-Enfleld. and that the majority of the men armed with the Ross rifle have not the confidence in it that is so essential they should possess. The inquiry on which these conclusions are based, was the outcome of an urgent application from a battalion of the third Canadian Division for re-armament with the short Lee-Enfleld rifle, in consequence of a high percentage of jams experienced with their Ross rifles during a hostile atack on the 1st May, 1916.
2.	I am accordingly of opinion that the second and third Canadian Divisions should be re-armed with the short Lee-Enfleld rifle. It will be remembered that the first Canadian Division was so re-armed on the 12th June, 1915.
3.	I am not in a position to effect this with the means at my disposal in France. I have the honour to inquire, therefore, whether the necessary number of rifles can be supplied from home sources, without interfering, or delaying, the arrival and arming of the divisions due from England and Egypt on which I am relying.
I have the honour to be,
Sir.
Your obedient Servant,
(Sgd.) D. Haig, General,
Commanding.in-Chief. British Armies in France,
Sir Douglas Haig, evidently on account of communications which- had passed between the Canadian Prime Minister and the Acting High Corrimissioner for Canada, was called upon for a second report. This report, dated June 21, 1916, is as follows:
Sir,-In reply to your No. 77/15/5307 (M.G.O.) of 10th June 1916, forwarding a copy of a telegram dated 7th June, from the Governor General of Canada, I have the honour to inform you that the efficiency of the Ross rifle has been thoroughly tested by actual fighting in the field, and the application conveyed in my O. B. /174 of 28th May 1916, was made after very careful consideration of all the evidence available.
2.	I have again consulted the General Officer Commanding Second Army in case any fresh points had come to light during the recent heavy fighting by the Canadians near Ypres. He tells me that his experience of the working of the Ross rifle during the last fight has only confirmed him in his/ opinion that the Canadians in the third Division, at all events, have lost confidence in their rifle and he recommends that the rifles in this division be exchanged.
3.	Although the reports from the Second Division are not to the same effect, I am of opinion that the Lee-Enfleld rifle should be issued to all three divisions of the Canadian Corps.
I must therefore adhere to my recommendation that the second and third Canadian divisions should be re-armed with the short Lee-Enfleld rifle, and I would urge the necessary steps to give effect thereto be taken without delay.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
(Sgd.) D. Haig, General,
Commanding-in-Chief, British Armies in France.

I wish to read also the following communication from Mr. Bonar Law to the Governor General of Canada, dated at London, July 11, 1916:
With reference to my telegram June 10th. Report from General Officer Commanding in Chief in France has now been received by Army Council recommending that second and third Canadian Divisions should be re-armed with short Dee-Enfleld rifles and Army Council have approved this. They hope to be able to utilize Ross rifles released and also those now in possession of Canadian troops in England for other purposes connected with the war_ but ask that no more Ross rifles should be brought to England. Army Council will be responsible for supplying necessary rifles to Canadian troops on arrival in England. If your Government desire to undertake manufacture of different rifles suitable for use during war, Army Council think that rifles now being produced in America for British Army on lines of Dee.Enfield Mark 111 but with improvements would be best.
(Sgd.) Bonar Daw.
This correspondence from the official file shows that on July 11, 1916, the British Government had decided, that no more Ross rifles should be used in the field, that they had all the Ross rifles in England that they required and that they specifically requested the Canadian Government to send no more of these rifles to England. There does not seem to be any intimation in the correspondence that the Ross rifle could be improved or changed so that it would meet the requirements of the War Office. I shall not go into the question of whether the chamber was too large or too small, or whether there was something wrong with the bolt, because probably every member has received or seen letters from so'diers at the front in which the defects were pointed out. In view of these facts, I think we have a right to ask the Government what course they intend to pursue. We have an army which, we are told, numbers about
400,000	men, and it is up to the Prime Minister and to every man in Canada to see that within the next six months that army shall number 500,000 men. These men will have to be armed. It is evident from the correspondence that since July 11, 1916, the British army has been looking after the arming of our troops in the field. The question arises: are we to continue to manuiac-ture rifles in Canada, or not? In the month of July last a statement appeared in the press to the effect that the Government had made arrangements with, the Ross Rifle Company for the manufacture of Lee-En-field rifles, and up to the last three or four weeks I believed that the Ross Rifle factory had been employed in that work. I have no official information on the subject,
but I am told that the Ross Rifle factory is not manufacturing Lee-Enfield rifles. Indeed, I am informed that no move has been made towards remodelling the Ross plant for the purpose of manufacturing Lee-Enfield rifles. According to the cablegram sent to the Prime Minister by the Acting High Commissioner, the remodelling of that plant for the manufacture of Lee-Enfields would involve an expenditure of only half a million dollars. In the United States they have been able to remodel a plant within, a very few months, get all the necessary tools, and turn out Lee-Enfield rifles in large quantities. The Government were advised eight months ago that if they wanted to continue the manufacture of rifles they should manufacture Lee-Enfields such as are turned out in the United States. Unless my information is very much at fault-I do not think it is, but if it is my right hon. friend will correct me-no attempt has been made to manufacture anything but Ross rifles. We have +lhe statement from the Prime Minister that the Government intend to continue manufacturing Ross rifles and an amount has been placed in the Estimates for the next year to provide for the. manufacture of 80,000 of them. The time has arrived when the Government should take the members of the House, the people of the country and, above all, the Canadian soldiers, into their confidence respecting their intentions as to the arming of our army. This is a question much bigger than a matter of dollars and cents. It goes to the very root of recruiting and of national confidence in our ability to play properly our part in winning this war. It is the most important thing which is before the Canadian public to-day, and until the matter is cleaned up recruiting will not be as it should be. I shall not dwell upon what Canadian soldiers have said in letters from the front; I do not think it would be patriotic to do so. Besides, these letters would not look good in print. While it is true that the soldier may grumble over a very small matter and that the Ross rifle may have been a very good arm in many ways, yet a prejudice has sprung up against the further continuance of the Ross rifle as the national arm of. Canada. If the Government are going to continue the manufacture of rifles, as I presume they are, they ought to tell us what they are going to do about it. Personally, I was not in Parliament when the contract with the Ross Rifle Company was made, but the matter

came up on very many occasions in 1905, 1906, and 1907, when I was in Parliament. I was always in favour of manufacturing rifles in Canada, and I am just as strongly in favour of manufacturing rifles in Canada to-day as I was in 1905, 1906, 1907 and 1908. The very fact that we have a factory in Canada that has turned out the finest target and sporting rifles in the world is evidence that we can manufacture rifles in Canada. The fact that we have in the city of Quebec a factory that has turned out 1,000 rifles a day is all the evidence we want that we can manufacture rifles, and on a very large scale. The whole difficulty with regard to the Ross rifle seem to be in the breech mechanism, something regarding the bolt and the chamber. While that is a very important part of the rifle, when it comes to the question of manufacture, to the cost of manufacture and to the complications of manufacture I Cannot see that it is at all an insurmountable difficulty. It seems to me that we have only to change over that portion of the chamber, and make a Lee-Enfield chamber, bolt and magazine, instead of a Ross bolt, chamber and magazine; and if we have the plant in which we can manufacture a rifle of any kind, surely we have a plant which, with a small additional expenditure, and with some application of brains and ability could manufacture the rifle which the British Government tell us they would like us to manufacture. They put it as plainly as the English language can make it. They would like this Government to enter into the manufacture of the improved Lee-Enfield rifle, the same as in the United States. We know that in twenty-four hours the British Government wouid furnish this Government with the sealed pattern, and with the standard rifle. I do not know how long it would take-I suppose it would take some months, but not very many months to convert our Ross factory into a Lee-Enfield factory.
I ask, and I do not think I am asking anything that is confidential, have the Government taken any steps to manufacture any other rifle than the Ross rifle in Canada ; have they taken any steps to convert the Ross rifle factory into a Lee-Enfield factory; have they done anything to get us out of the unfortunate position in which we find ourselves; or are they simply going to manufacture 80.000 more rifles in Canada and turn out an arm which, according to ithe official representations, does not inspire our troops with confidence, and _which is not taken to England at the re-
quest of the British Government.
I hope the Prime Minister will appreciate that I approach this question in no controversial spirit. I have not tried to go into any of the difficulties that have existed heretofore. I ajm simply asking him, in the interests of Canada, and in the interests of the ttoops of Canada, whether he will take the country and the House into his confidence and tell us what the Government have done. I think I might go so far as to ask him to tell us what they propose to do, and whether they intend, in the first place, to carry on the manufacture of rifles an Canada, and if so, whether it is to be the Ross or the Lee-Enfield rifle

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the request of the hon. gentleman is a very reasonable one, and I entirely appreciate the spirit in which he has approached the subject, and the general tone of his remarks in regard to this very important matter. The merits of the Ross rifle have been a matter of discussion in this House on various occasions during the past ten years. I recollect very well when I was on the other side of the House-I think my hon. friend was rot then in. Parliament.

I was. I was not a
member when the contract was signed, but I was here during all the discussions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recollect then the various reports that were placed before the country and their general character. I do not think there was any doubt in the minds of members that, as a marksman's rifle, there was no better rifle in the world than the Ross rifle. I recollect that the consideration which impressed me at the time was whether or not the rifle as then ordered was of a sufficiently strong type to endure successfully the wear and tear of active service. I believe that certain portions of the rifle, which were thought to be weak, were afterwards strengthened, and the contract was acted upon Rifles were ordered from time to time, and thus the situation presented itself to the present Administration at the outbreak of war.
It might be proper for a moment to advert to the contract which was made by the former Government and which had to ,be taken into account by the present Government when it came to deal with, the .question. I am not referring to this by way

of reproach, but merely in order that the House may be possessed of the character of the contract that was made, and thus be enabled to understand what the contractual position was as between the Government, on the one hand, and the Ross Rifle Company on the other. The contract reads as follows:
Memorandum of Agreement made in duplicate this 27th day of March 1902.
Between
Sir Charles Ross, Bart., of Balnagowan, hereinafter called the Contractor, of the first part, and
His Majesty the King, represented by Honourable F. W. Borden, Minister of Militia and Defence for the Dominion of Canada, hereinafter called the minister, which expression as herein used includes also the successors in office of the said Minister of Militia and Defence, His Majesty so represented being hereinafter referred to as the Government, of the second part.
Whereas it is considered in the general interests of Canada that the rifles required by the Government for the purposes of Militia and Defence should be manufactured in Canada and whereas the contractor has proposed by himself or his assigns to undertake the establishment and operation of a suitable factory in Canada for the manufacture of such rifles, and to supply the Government with the rifles so required manufactured at said factory and delivered at a cost to the Government, not exceeding that which the Government would have to pay for similar rifles purchased by or for the Government as heretofore in the English market.
This agreement therefore witnesseth, and it is agreed by and between the Contractor and the Government, as follows:-
1.	The contractor is to establish at or near the city of Quebec in Canada a factory for the manufacture of rifles, with the necessary plant.
2.	The contractor undertakes to deliver to the Government between the first day of January. 1903, and tlje first day of January 1904, 12,000 rifles manufactured at the said factory corresponding and equal in every respect to a standard sample rifle which is to be approved by the minister, such rifles to be delivered by monthly even quantities, as nearly as may be of 1,000.
3.	The Government shall be bound and entitled to purchase from the contractor all rifles required for the use of the Government during the continuance of this contract. The contractor agrees that if the Government so desires and signifies its desire in writing on or before the 30th day of September in any year after the year now current, the contractor will deliver to the Government within the year following the next succeeding first day of January a number of rifles not less than 10,000 manufactured at the said factory, such rifles to be delivered by monthly even quantities, as nearly as may be, of not less than 800. If during the year the Government shall require any number of rifles in excess of the number hereinbefore specified for that year, the Government shall immediately notify the contractor of the additional number required, and the contractor shall do his utmost to manufacture at the said factory and to deliver to the Government all such rifles as may be reasonably required, and if need be he shall operate the factory at any time twenty four
hours per day, and he shall if required, furnish the total output of the said factory to the gov-vernment; provided however, that in case of war, actual or threatened, or any national emergency, requiring in the opinion of the Government, the immediate supply of additional arms, the contractor upon receiving any notice or demand from the Government for any number of rifles specified to be urgently required in view of this proviso shall, within thirty days after receiving such notice or demand notify the Government in writing of the number of rifles which he will undertake to furnish in accordance with such notice or demand, and the Government shall not under any circumstances be bound to purchase from the contractor in respect of any such notice or demand, any number of rifles in excess of the number which the contractor so notifies the Government that he will be able to supply.
4.	All the said rifles hereby contracted for are previous to delivery to be inspected by the Inspector of Small Arms of the Government of Canada, and upon such inspection the same rifles being found up to sample as aforesaid, delivery shall be taken as complete at the factory.
5.	If at any time or from time to time, the Government should desire to have any changes in or modification of the rifle to be manufactured and supplied by the contractor, the Government may give to the contractor at least twelve months notice in writing, specifying such changes or modification, and requiring the contractor at the expiration of the period of such notice to manufacture and deliver rifles so changed or modified, and the contractor shall therupon be bound upon and after the expiration of the said period, to manufacture and deliver the rifles subject to such changes and modifications, and the said standard sample rifle so furnished as aforesaid shall in respect of all rifles to be delivered after the expiration of the said period be deemed to have been altered or modified in accordance with the changes or modification specified by the said notice.
C. If a new rifle shall be invented which the Government shall desire to adopt or use the Government may furnish to the contractor a standard sample of such new rifle, and give the contractor twelve months notice in writing, requiring that the rifles to be delivered by the contractor upon and after the expiration of the period of such last mentioned notice shall correspond to the standard sample of such new rifle so furnished, the Government to protect the contractor against any actions for infringements of patents so far as such new rifles supplied to the Government are concerned, and upon and after the expiration of the said period all rifles to be delivered by the contractor shall accordingly correspond to such substituted standard sample, and the contractor agrees to originally lay out and adapt his plant, machinery etc., so as to provide the best facilities winch can reasonably be foreseen to enable him to apply the same to the manufacture of any such new rifle which may be desired.
7.	The Government shall furnish to the contractor. a standard sample rifle mentioned in the second clause of this contract, on or before the 10th day of April, 1902. If for any reason such standard rifle should not be furnished until after the said date, the said contractor shall, if he so desires, be entitled to equivalent extension of the time herein provided for manufacture and delivery.
8.	The Government shall pay for the said 12,000 rifles mentioned in the second clause of

this contract at the rate of $25 for each such rifle. The Government shall pay out of the moneys to be appropriated by Parliament for the purpose for all rifles subsequently ordered as herein stipulated the same price of $25 for each of such rifles, unless one of the parties hereto shall upon the occasion of any such demand for further rifles notify the other of such parties that the price of such rifles in similar quantities in the markets of Great Britain has relatively to the present time increased or diminished, in which case the aforesaid price of $25 shall no longer govern, but the price for the rifles so ordered and to be thereafter ordered shall depend upon a further agreement of the parties, and in default of agreement the price to be fixed as provided in the 9th clause hereof. The price of all rifles herein contracted for or to be supplied pursuant to the provisions of this agreement shall be payable upon delivery; provided however, that after the establishment of the said factory and supplying of the plant for the running of the same, the contractor shall be entitled to payment in advance of delivery of moneys actually expended upon the rifles or parts thereof or fixtures therefor, to be delivered in that year upon a statement certified by him of the amount so spent upon establishing the fact of such expenditures to the satisfaction, testified by his signature of such statement, of the Government Inspector of Small Arms, such payments in no case to exceed 75 per cent, of the price of such rifles, the contractor undertaking whenever such advances are made, to insure and keep insured said rifles, parts and fixtures against loss or damage by fire for the benefit of the Government to the extent of such advances.
9.	Provided, however, that in case of any
changes in or modification of the rifle to be manufactured by the contractor, hereunder, pursuant to any such notice as aforesaid, or in case of the adoption by the Government of a new rifle to be invented as aforesaid, the price to be paid shall be the price above named, or such price increased or diminished by a sum to be agreed upon between the Government and the contractor, having regard to the question as to whether such changes or modification increase or diminish the cost of production, or in the case of the adoption of a new rifle, a price to be agreed upon between the Government and the contractor; provided, further, that in default of agreement, the amount of such increase or diminution of the price, as the case may be, shall be settled by two experts, one of whom shall be chosen by the Government, and the other by the contractor, whose decision, if unanimous, shall be final, while in the event of a difference between them the two experts so named shall name a third, and the decision of any two of the three shall be binding; it being the intention of this agreement that the price of the rifles furnished hereunder shall so far as is possible be the same as that of similar rifles in like quantities purchased by or for the Government from the British manufacturers in the open market in England and delivered in Ottawa.	.
10.	The contractor shall be permitted to import into Canada all tools and machinery not manufactured in Canada up to the required standard necessary for the said factory, and also all material, or parts in the rough, unfinished, to be used in rifles to be manufae-

tured by him for the Government free of duty, or in the case of payment by the contractor of any duty on any such tools, machinery or material or parts aforesaid, the contractor shall be entitled to a drawback or remission of the amount so paid; provided, also, that the contractor shall be entitled to import free of duty or shall be entitled to drawback or remission of duty paid in respect of the finished parts to be used in any such rifles, consisting of screws, nuts, bands and springs; and provided, further, that	if at any
time during the continuance of this contract the demand of the Government for rifles shall be such as to make it necessary for the contractor to enlarge the capacity of his factory then the machinery plant and material imported by him for that purpose, not manufactured in Canada up to the required standard, shall similarly be entitled to free entry, drawback or remission of duty.
11.	The contractor shall not be bound to deliver at the time specified in the case of strike or in the event of unforeseen occurrences beyond his control preventing manufacture, but in such cases the contractor shall have an equivalent extension of time, he hereby undertaking to resume work as soon as possible.
12.	The standard sample rifle to be approved by the minister, as provided in paragraph 2 of this agreement, and all standard samples substituted therefor pursuant to this agreement shall remain in the custody of the minister.
13.	Any notice to the contractor, hereunder, shall be deemed to be well and sufficiently given if the same be left at the contractor's office or mailed in any post office to the contractor at the said factory.
14.	This contract is hereby, pursuant to the provisions of the 16th section of chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, made subject to the express condition that no member of the House of Commons of Canada shall be admitted to any share or part of such contract or to any benefit to be derived therefrom.
15.	This contract shall enure to the benefit of and shall be binding on the executors, administrators and assigns of the contractor, and where the context admits any reference, therein to the contractor shall be taken to extend equally to his executors, administrators and! assigns.
16.	The wages to be paid in the execution of this contract shall be those generally accepted as current in each trade for competent working men and working women in the district where the work is carried out.
In witness whereof the contractor and the minister have hereunder set their hands and seals at Ottawa aforesaid the day and year first above written.
Signed, sealed and delivered in the presence of (Sgd.) Charles D. Ross (seal) (Sgd.) R. F. Pinault.
(Sgd.) F. W. Borden (seal) Minister of Militia and Defence.
The contract, after it was made, was assigned with the sanction of the Government to the Ross Rifle Company, and at the present time it is therefore a contract between the Ross Rifle ' Company, the assignee of Sir Charles Ross, and the Government of Canada. I have read the contract in order that it might be known from ite terms that

no period was fixed for its termination. The Government is advised that the contract therefore continues indefinitely, the Government having no power to bring it to a conclusion.
I appreciate the fact, and I do not want to minimize it, that the contractor, Sir Charles Ross, and the company which he afterwards organized, were required to incur a very considerable expenditure in establishing a rifle plant in Canada, and it was therefore necessary to give them a contract of long duration, as otherwise no person could be expected to invest his capital in this country for such a purpose, considering that the company would have to depend, outside of its contract with the Government, upon such orders as they might be able to obtain for sporting and other rifles not designed for military purposes. The rifle has gone through various stages of development. First of all there was the Mark 1, as to which some criticism was made, and there were suggestions as to its improvement by expert officers of the Government. The defects, whatever they may have been, pointed out in that way, were supposed to be remedied by the adoption of the rifle known as Mark II. Criticism having also arisen of that rifle, and certain defects having been found, an endeavour was made to eliminate them by the adoption of the Mark III, which is the rifle mentioned in the correspondence that my hon. friend the member from Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) has read.
Now, the Ross rifle factory was the only factory in Canada capable of producing rifles for military purposes when the war began. As a matter of fact this should be said, and it is to the credit of Sir Charles Ross and of the Ross Rifle Company that it can be said, that, after the outbreak of war, I understand that factory was more successful in greatly increasing its output than any other factory on this continent. I believe that the increased output which that factory developed in at least the first year and a half of the war was very much greater than the increase in output which was shown by .any of the great rifle factories in the United States.
With regard to the extent of orders given by the Government, I might as well clear that point up at once, and the House is certainly entitled to the information. The Government of Canada have ordered since the outbreak of the war 290,000 rifles, and the Ross Rifle Company has delivered to the Government of Canada since the outbreak of the war 218,547 Tifles. There remains to be delivered 97,590 rifles, upon orders already .given.
There seems some discrepancy there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, there is
an explanation here. The discrepancy in the figures is due to an order for 30,000 rifles which was placed before the war, and of these 26,137 were delivered after the outbreak of the war.
Let me refer for a moment to the .situation as it presented itself to the Government in the summer of 1915. My h.on. friend and other hon. gentlemen have referred to the criticism which Sir John French made of the rifle, and I think it is just as well at this stage that I should allude specifically to Sir John French's report, because in the light of that report the House and the country must judge of the steps which the Government took when that report had been communicated to them, and when, in consequence of it, the first Canadian division was armed with the Lee-Enfield instead of the Ross rifle.
1 want to emphasise that point right here; I do not want hon. members in this House or any one in the country to forget it. Whenever we were told by the competent authorities at the front that it was in the interest of the Canadian soldiers that the Lee-Enfield rifle should be substituted for the Ross rifle on any occasion, the Government of Canada have always assented and placed themselves within the judgment of the military authorities at the front who ought to know better in respect of such matters than we, sitting around a council board at Ottawa, could possibly know. So, when it was proposed in the summer of 1915 that the First Division should be re-armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle, for the reasons stated in Sir John French's report, we, of course, interposed no objection, and the First Division was re-armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle. Let us see what Sir John French said about the rifle. His report which has been brought down and laid on the table of the House is as follows:
Confidential.
From the Field Marshal, Commanding in Chief, British Army in the Field, to the Secretary, War Office, London, S.W., General Headquarters, June 19, 1915.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of War Office letter No. 77-15-5209 (A.5), dated 16-6-1915, regarding the action taken by

me in the matter of the Ross rifles of the Canadian Division.
2.	The circumstances are as follows:-
I had heard rumours that there was a growing want of confidence in this rifle, as evidenced by the fact that the infantry of the Canadian Division were taking every opportunity of exchanging their rifles with those of the Lee-En-field pattern from casualties on the battlefield.
3.	To satisfy myself whether there was any real justification for this state of affairs, without at the same time lending encouragement to the idea that the Ross rifle was unsatisfactory, such as might have resulted from an investigation by the divisional authorities, I gave instructions for the assembly of a small committee at my general headquarters to test the rifle with the various natures of ammunition in use, including ammunition of Canadian manufacture, of which a small supply was obtained from England for the purpose, none having been sent out to this country for use with rifle.
4.	The proceedings of this committee were
laid before me on the eve of a serious offensive operation in which the Canadian Division was to take part, and I was at the same time informed that over 3,000, or more than one-third of the infantry, of this division had already succeeded in re-arming themselves with the Dee-Enfield rifle without any authority having been given for them to do so.	.
Looking:
(1)	To the unanimous opinion of my committee that the Ross rifle could not be relied upon to work smoothly and efficiently in rapid fire with any ammunition other than that of Canadian manufacture;
(2)	to the fact that no ammunition of this nature was available in this country, and that sufficient supplies could not be obtained from England, and,
(3)	to the want of confidence in the rifle which a large number of the infantry evidently felt, as evidenced by the fact that over 3,000 had, without authority, exchanged their rifles for those used by their British comrades, and taken from casualties on the battlefield.
I did not feel justified in sending this Division into battle with the Ross rifle, and ordered the re-arming of the infantry of the Division with the Lee-Enfield rifle, which was carried out before they went into action on the 15th instant;
5.	As regards the suggestion made by the Army Council that the opinion of one or two selected Canadian officers should be obtained, I submit that this is a difficult and complicated question which can only be satisfactorily settled by the best expert opinion, and that the views of a few selected Canadian officers, who may or may not be prejudiced in the matter, will not be of any material assistance.
6.	I wrould, therefore, suggest that the Army Council should send to this country one or more of the most highly qualified experts obtainable to make the necessary tests under service conditions and report whether ammunition of British manufacture is or is not suitable for use with the Ross rifle. For this purpose a supply of ammunition of Canadian manufacture should be brought out for comparison.
The Army Council can then decide whether, looking to all the circumstances, it is advisable to restore the Ross rifle to the Canadian Divisions.
7.	In conclusion, I would observe that in my reports I have never condemned the Ross rifle, nor have I any sufficient data to justify me in doing so.
fSir Robert Borden. 1
I have expressed and acted on my opinion, that, so far as I can judge, the ammunition of British manufacture is not suitable for use with Ross rifles, and that there is a large and growing feeling of want of confidence in their rifle on the part of the men in the Canadian Division, which is amply justified by the report of the committee.
8.	Owing to the difficulty at present experienced in turning out rifles in sufficient numbers for our requirements, I shall most heartily welcome an authoritative statement which will carry conviction to the men that their apprehensions are unfounded, or what may possibly be found more easy of attainment, viz.: a slight alteration to the chamber of the rifle which will better adapt it for use with our British ammunition.
I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant,
(Signed) J. D. P. French.

Before the right hon. gentleman goes any further on that point, I would like to ask if the Government was ever furnished with the report of the experts whom General French stated he intended to bring over from Great Britain?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am under the impression-I shall obtain accurate information on that-that we did not receive the report to which my hon. friend has alluded.

The article that appeared in the newspaper in the month of May last has, I think, been referred to as the Alderson report. Was that report in the hands of the Government, and would that possibly be the experts' report to which General French referred to?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand it, the communication to which my hon. friend alludes was a private letter from General Alderson to General Gwatkin; it was not an official document at all. In some mysterious way, which has never been explained, and without the authority or knowledge of General Gwatkin, a copy was taken and was given or solid to some person outside of the department altogether, and was made public. I did not know anything about it, so far as my recollection goes, until I saw it in the newspapers. No copy was ever furnished to me, and I do not know whether a copy was ever furnished to the ex-Minister of Militia.

My memory is that at a certain time during last session when a discussion in regard to the Ross rifle was going on, I asked the Prime Minister if he would lay on the table an official report by a board of inquiry made in England which was mentioned at the time. He declined to do so on the ground of military disadvantage if it were done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In so far as my hon. friend's questions do not have immediate reference to the subject we are discussing, if he will kindly make a note of them and permit me to continue the thread of my remarks, I shall be grateful. It is difficult to deal with interruptions that are not precisely relevant.
The situation which confronted the Government in the summer of 1915 was this: We knew that Sir John French had concluded that the First Canadian Division ought to be re-armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle. He based that conclusion very largely upon the consideration that the men of the First Division, or a considerable number of them, had lost confidence in the Ross rifle. He took the view, in which I am sure we all concur, that no rifle, however effective, would be useful to the men if they had lost confidence in it. He said, in that same report, that he did not condemn the Ross rifle-that he had no data upon which he could condemn it; and he said further that the difficulty had arisen by reason of the fact that the ammunition supplied in this country, which might have made the rifle useful, could not be supplied in sufficient quantities. We algo knew that the chief difficulty at the front was from the jamming of the cartridges, and that is alluded to by Sir John French' in the concluding paragraph of his report when he himself makes the suggestion that if other rifles cannot be provided a remedy might be found by altering the chamber of the rifle, enlarging it so that the cartridge would not stick. We were also confronted with the fact that we did not then know of any other source from which we could procure rifles for the arming of our troops. It may be_ suggested that we should have given notice to manufacture the Lee-Enfield rifle. Well, it took something more than three months, according to my recollection, to get a sealed sample of the rifle that, as I shall point out later on, was suggested by the War Office as the new standard rifle for this country. I first asked in September, 1916, that a sample rifle for the purpose of making the cnange snouict De lurnished. We did not receive it until January. Wie were confronted with the further consideration that under the terms of the contract the contractors were permitted the full period of one year before they could be called upon to produce rifles of a different type. We also had information from the British
Government, whom we consulted on the subject, that a period of considerably more than a year would undoubtedly elapse, in their opinion, before the Ross rifle factory could be changed and the new plant acquired to enable them to produce a rifle of another type. In connection with that we had to take into account, of course, the extreme demands which were being made upon all the resources of this continent for plant and machinery of every kind, the lack of suitable steel, the great delay attending the filling of orders for machinery of any kind, and the fact that the machinery for turning out rifles is of a highly varied and complex character. So that, even if a contract were undertaken to deliver at a certain time, no one could be absolutely sure that it would be delivered within the period mentioned. And the war would not wait for these people, whoever they might be, to perfect their arrangements and secure their plant and machinery.
We must bear in mind, further, that in June and July, 1915, people in this country were not as thoroughly impressed with the possible duration of this war as they are to-day. I have already stated publicly that when I came back from Great Britain and communicated to some of my colleagues and to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) my belief that the British Empire would not be able to throw its full strength into this struggle before June, 1916, every one of them was greatly surprised, and some could hardly credit the accuracy of the impression I had thus formed. We were looking forward then to a conclusion of the war some time in 1916; and as matters lay before us then, it did not seem possible that we could produce rifles of the Lee-Enfield type before the probable date of the conclusion of the war.
But then, further, the jamming difficulty was not confined to the Ross rifle, it affected the Lee-Enfield rifle as well. I do not know whether it affected the Lee-iinfield to the same degree as it affected the Ross, but of this I am perfectly confident, on information communicated to me by my late colleague the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) and others, that there was serious difficulty with the Lee-Enfield rifle itself in using the ammunition that was furnished. We came to the conclusion that the only course for us to pursue was to enlarge the chamber of the Ross rifle with a view to preventing the

cartridge from jamming. The size of the chamber, as I am informed, had been fixed originally at 463. If I am not mistaken,
. that was done in 1908. Afterwards, in 1910, it was reduced to '457, and about Januaiy, 1911, it was fixed at .460. Now, the British ammunition is precisely the same-.460. so, you had a cartridge which fitted tightly in the chamber of the rifle, and if the least bit of dirt should adhere to the cartridge before it went into the chamber, the jamming of the cartridge was inevitable.
What did we do? In view of what Sir John French had said, and in view of the experience of the men at the front, we decided that our only course was to enlarge the chamber of the Boss rifle. In July, 1915, it was decided to enlarge the chamber to *462, which is the diameter of the chamber of the Lee-Enfield rifle. But the then Minister of Militia and Defence, on looking into the matter more carefully, came to the conclusion that, for the purpose of absolutely preventing if possible, any danger of jamming, he had better go a little further: and so, in August, 1915, he directed that the chamber should be enlarged to [DOT] 464. That was done, and, as I understand it, the Second Division, when it went to the front, was armed with the Ross rifle with the enlarged chamber.
Did the Small Arms Commission recommend the last change to * 462?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed by the deputy minister that the Small Arms Commission did recommend that change.
Did the Small Arms Commission recommend the change from -462 to -457?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I really could not tell my hon. friend that. I obtained the information not from the department, but from what I regarded as a reliable source. I had not time to verify it, but I will do so and see whether I am correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where was the last enlargement made-''

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The enlargement was carried on in Great Britain. I have fairly full reports as to all that took place with regard to that, but I will not deal with that phase of the matter just at the moment. I shall be prepared, however, to do so later if my right hon. friend desires it.

Was the question
considered of making ammunition in Canada which would fit the chamber?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that at the beginning of the war the only ammunition production that we could rely upon was that of the Dominion Arsenal, which, of course, was trivial as compared with the need. Afterwards we made contracts. The ammunition that was produced in this country was, as I am informed by the Deputy Minister of Militia, sent forward and pooled with the British ammunition, this country being given credit for it. Then the troops at the front were supplied by the general ordnance organization, as there could not be a separate ordnance arrangement for the Canadian troops in France. Unless, therefore, we attempted to carry out an apparently impracticable project, that of having a separate Canadian ordnance department for the Canadian troops at the front, we could not rely upon Canadian ammunition being served out to the Canadian troops. It seemed impossible to make that arrangement.
Will the Prime Minister state what was the result of enlarging the bore of the rifle in England?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The result was supposed to be satisfactory, so far as the jamming was concerned. My hon. friend has before him the report of Sir Douglas Haig, to which I will refer in a moment. The Second Division went to the front on September 13, 1915, and as the enlargement of the chambers of the Ross rifle had not proceeded to a sufficient extent to enable the men of that Division to be armed with the Ross, they went to the front, as I am informed, armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle. The Third Division began to go to the front in January, 1916. By the end of February, 1916, nearly the whole division was at the front; the Engineer and Artillery units, however, went later. The whole division was in France at the end of June.
In February, 1916, the question arose as to whether further orders should be given for the Ross rifle and, if so, to what extent. The Government had before them a recommendation from the Master-General of the Ordnance for 200,000 Roes rifles, if I remember correctly. We did not accede to that in the whole; we gave an order for
100,000	Ross rifles with the enlarged chambers. In March, 1916, when the question came up as to the remaining portion of
