We were looking around at that time, in view of an earlier termination of the war than now seems probable, to see whether or not provision could be made by which further very large orders for the Ross rifle should not be necessary. We realized that with the orders already outstanding :a very large supply of rifles would be in the hands of the Government at the end of the war. Having regard to the fact that during the previous summer the question of jamming had arisen, and also to some further rumours that came to our [DOT]attention, we considered that it might be better, if it were possible, to make provision that the Canadian troops be supplied with standard British rifles to which no objection had been taken. We were, however, informed at that time, April 26, that no such provision could be made; therefore we had to consider the situation from that standpoint.
These rumours, to which I have alluded, began to assume more definite shape, and I saw a telegram on the 12th May, 1916, from Sir Max Aitken to General Hughes, a portion o'f which has been brought down, and which was as follows:
Serious situation has arisen regarding Ross rifle *	*	[DOT] I request that you will show this
telegram to Prime Minister.
To this I replied on the 15th of May, two days, I think, before the Alderson report,
so-called, had made its appearance in the press. That report appeared on the 17th of May, but on the 15th of May I had sent to Sir Max Aitken the following telegram:
Have consulted with General Hughes and we are prepared to leave matter to judgment of Commander in Chief after he has had all necessary tests of both rifles under such conditions as are experienced at front. Men making tests should be of like experience.
It is only arm we are equipped to produce in Canada at present and we believe it effective if properly used. Minister Informs me that reports just received of recent official tests in England thoroughly demonstrate efficiency of our rifle.
I had discussed the subject with General Hughes, and he had given me that assurance and expressed very great confidence in the efficiency of the rifle, if properly used. I may say here that the test to which the Ross rifle was subjected was one of very great severity. It was a longer rifle than the Lee-Enfield, and that interfered, perhaps, to some extent with its use in the trenches. No one before the outbreak of the war, or in the early months of the war, could have foreseen that trench warfare would dominate the situation to the extent which it did. Further than that, the use of rifles, in trench warfare, with the mud a foot, or two or three feet deep, with rifles falling into the mud and becoming dirty-all that was a particularly severe test of the Ross rifle which was of higher quality in many respects than the Lee-Enfield rifle. It was put to a further severe test in this way:	It was placed in the
hands of men who were not trained soldiers, men as gallant and splendid as the world ever produced, but men who were not trained soldiers, who naturally were not trained as efficiently as the men of a regular army would be in the care of their weapons. Therefore, the conditions of the test to which the Ross rifle was subjected were of an unusually severe character. I am not at all sure that with an enlarged chamber, and under ordinary conditions of warfare, the Ross rifle would not be found a thoroughly efficient weapon. But the question with which we were always confronted was whether the men had confidence in it. Once we were convinced that they had not confidence in it, we agreed immediately that they must be armed with a rifle in which they had confidence, or they could not be effective.
In pursuance of these communications, I sent on the 5th day of June, 1916, a telegram to Sir William Robertson, Chief of the General Staff. It was sent through the

Governor General to the Secretary of State for the Colonies. That telegram read:
Secret. Following from the Prime Minister for Sir William Robertson. By reason of rumoured dissatisfaction with Ross rifle I held consultation with General Hughes on May 15 and sent unofficial message to Commander in Chief that we were prepared to leave matter to his judgment after making all necessary tests of both rifles under such conditions as are experienced at the front. We suggested that men making tests should be of equal experience. Ross rifle is only arm we are equipped to produce in Canada at present and we believe it efficient if properly used but are content to abide by judgment of Commander in Chief after thorough investigation and adequate tests. We realize absolute necessity of two conditions: first, that men shall be armed with thoroughly efficient rifle; second, that their confidence in such rifle shall be unshaken Please let me have your judgment as to proper course to pursue
On the same day I sent to Sir George Perley, who had taken a very keen and active interest in the matter, this telegram:
Confidential. Please ask Colonial Secretary to show you my secret cable to-day for Chief General Staff respecting Ross rifle and confer with Aitken to whom you may disclose terms of that message.
On the 5th day of June, I also sent to Sir George Perley the following telegram:
Secret. Please ascertain whether British Government have finally and definitely decided on new rifle, or whether they propose before final action to study lessons obtained in present war. If new type of rifle has been finally adopted we are prepared after suitable investigation to adopt it if found satisfactory, so that our rifle in future will be of same type as British. In that case British order for Ross rifles might be cancelled and new order for one hundred thousand rifles new type given Instead. Cost of machines and gauges for new type of rifle would approximate five hundred thousand dollars and this cost might be equally divided between two governments. Am making this suggestion because of continued criticism of Ross rifle which undoubtedly creates lack of confidence. No rifle however efficient is useful unless it commands thorough confidence of men.
I notice that in the communication which my right hon. friend has just Tead, he referred to the fact that the British Government had given an order for Ross rifles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am coming to that now.
Perhaps my right hon. friend could tell us whether that order is still in existence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall go into that fully. In the early months of this war we had a good deal of communication with

the British Government as to the supply of rifles. The question was surrounded with much difficulty, and some of the calculations made at that time were not justified by subsequent events. The British Government took up the question of obtaining Titles in Canada, and in the autumn of 1914 they ordered 100,000 Ross rifles. I have asked for and obtained a memorandum as to what has been accomplished by the Ross Rifle Company in supplying rifles under that order. The memorandum which has been given to me by the Department of Militia and Defence is as follows:
Number ordered for the War Office, 100,000 ; number delivered to 20th January, 1917, 48,8C0 ; number still to be delivered, 51,200.
The Ross Rifle Company is still engaged in the production of those rifles for the British Government. It will be observed from the telegram which I have just read that I made a certain suggestion to the British Government in that regard. I suggested to them in effect this: There has been criticism of the Ross rifle; we are told that the men have lost confidence in it; you have an outstanding contract for the Ross rifle; we have outstanding contracts fpr the Ross rifle; the cost of the new machinery to make the necessary changes will be $500,000 (as a matter of fact, I think it would have been a great deal more than that); would it not be better for the two Governments to arrange with the Ross Rifle Company to cease the production of Ross rifles, and to change the orders, in so far as they have not been fulfilled, to the Lee-Enfield rifle, or the type of new rifle which is now being produced for you in the United States? That was the suggestion, which, however, the British Government did not accept.

What was the date of
that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The 5th day of
June, 1916.

Did the Government, or any of its officials, ever receive from the British Government an offer of machinery and the different tools necessary to re-equip the Ross Rifle factory for the purpose of manufacturing Lee-Enfields?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We asked them about experts. They said that in so far as some dies, machinery and plant were concerned, they would be procured and placed at our service for use in the production of a new rifle.
When?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot recall that but I will find out. Sir George Perley advised us on the 8th of June:
London, June 8th, 1916.
***War Office considers except trajectory the new Lee-Enfield now being made in United States is as good as any weapon that could be made with present experience and in present war; apparently high trajectory no particular disadvantage. Lessons obtained in present war have evidently not brought any new experience so far as rifles are concerned. Not considered possible say definitely what rifle will be finally adopted by British Government after war. Hardly to be expected that War Office would under present circumstances definitely commit themselves regarding their future service rifle. Master General Ordnance considers rifle now being made for them in United States exceedingly good weapon and would be glad see you use same pattern. Question of money arrangements would have to be taken up officially*but personally should consider that of minor importance.
Then, in reply to a previous telegram as to the test of the Ross rifle, I had from Sir George Perley, on the 8th June, 1916, this telegram already laid on the table of the House:
London, June 8th, 1916.
Confidential. Have shown and discussed with Aitken your secret cable to Chief General Staff.
-that is the telegram to Sir William Robertson which I have already read-
Question will now doubtless be settled by him. Have seen him personally to-day and impressed strongly as possible upon him your views regarding necessity thorough test and also that Canadian Government would need official documents giving full facts and statements which could be made public if thought desirable. Also impressed upon him that Ross rifle is only one which Canada can produce at present and that if our troops are re-armed at front it naturally would raise question whether Canada should continue manufacturing Ross rifle an'd if not some alternative feasible plan would have to be suggested. Showed him copy your cable 5th regarding new type rifle which I answered this morning. Whole question will doubtless be thoroughly considered within next few days.
Then, on the 10th of June, in reply to my telegram to Sir William Robertson, I had this communication through the Secretary of State for the Colonies. It is a telegram addressed to the Governor General:
The following, from the Chief of the Imperial General Staff. Begins :
I am much obliged for your telegram 6th June. It has been referred to Sir Douglas Haig and his reply is awaited before ahy opinion can be given.
On the 24th June I sent this telegram to Sir George Perley:
26 _
Most confidential, Secret. We have had under consideration since January last an order for one hundred thousand additional Ross rifles, none of which can be delivered before April, 1917. If we decide to order the additional one hundred thousand company requires nearly a year's notice before commencement of delivery in order to secure necessary material of various kinds for which there is great demand at present. Several months ago the Master General of Ordnance strongly recommended immediate action, but we have delayed by reason of doubts raised as to efficiency of rifle. Time has now arrived when immediate decision should be made. To this end it is important that we should have a definite, reliable and thorough report upon the merits of rifle. If it is so defective as to forbid its use at the front, or if confidence in its efficiency has been undermined in our troops, it would be a waste of public money to give further orders. Please consult Aitken, with whom I have had much correspondence on this subject and advise me whether any such report as above mentioned exists. If not, it should be made immediately for our guidance.
On the 5th of July I received from Sir George Perley a telegram as follows:
London, July 5th, 1916.
Your cable 24th ultimo. Have communication from War Office covering letters recently received from commander in chief armies in Prance who reports efficiency Ross rifle thoroughly tested by actual fighting in field, that he has again consulted general officer commanding second army in case fresh points have come to light during recent heavy fighting by Canadians near Ypres. Latter states his experience working Ross rifle during last fight has only confirmed his opinion that Canadians in Third Division have lost confidence in their rifle and he reccommends that rifles this Division be exchanged. Sir Douglas Haig remarks that although reports from Second Division not to same effect he is of opinion Lee-Enfleld rifle should be issued to all three Divisions Canadian corps. Army Council agree with this opinion and have approved his proposal to exchange rifles Second and Third Divisions for Lee-Enfleld pattern and steps will be taken forthwith effect exchange. Army Cduncil hope be hble utilize Ross rifles released from France, also those in possession Canadian troops England, for other purposes connected with war. They would be glad if steps could be taken stop any more Ross rifles being brought to England, it being understood they thereby make themselves responsible for supplying necessary rifles to Canadian troops on arrival here and they see no reason to doubt being able do this. Army Council add should Canadian Government be desirous undertaking manufacture rifle of different pattern suitable for use during present war, in their opinion rifle made same pattern as now produced in United States for British Army, which is on lines Lee-Enfield Mark III embodying improvements, probably best one to adopt. Mailing copies correspondence. War Office wishes this matter regarded as secret until July 15th.
It will be observed that the improved British rifle, what is known as the Enfield 1914 rifle, was not being produced in Great Britain; it was only being produced in the United States. The standard Lee-Enfield rifle was being produced in Great Britain.



but in the United States a new plant and a new organization had to he created. The improved type of rifle could be produced as quickly as the old type. The Enfield 19T4 rifle had a -276 bore instead of -303 bore; it was impossible to adhere to the -276 bore, for the reason that the ammunition 'being produced in England would not be suitable for that rifle; therefore, they took the new improved type, the 1914 Enfield rifle, and adapted the barrel to a -303 calibre and that is the rifle for which they have made contracts in the United States.
Would that not require a new chamber?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The chamber, as I understand, is included in the barrel. At all events, that is what I am informed by the technical officer. The improvements effected in the new type, called the Enfield 1914, which was practically, but not formally, adopted before war broke out, were utilized and adopted in the orders given in the United States, but the barrel was of a [DOT] 303 calibre and not a -276 calibre.
Then follow in order certain documents which my hon. friend has referred to, and which I khould like again to place before the House. I need not read Mr. Cubitt's letter. I will read Sir Douglas Haig's report, dated May 28, 1916:
May 28, 1916.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that 1 have satisfied myself, after extensive inquiries carried out throughout the Canadian Corps, that, as a service rifle, the Ross is less trustworthy than the Lee-Enfield, and that the majority of the men armed with the Ross rifle have not the confidence in it that it is so essential [DOT] that they should possess. The inquiry on which these conclusions are based, was the outcome of an urgent application from a battalion of the 3rd Canadian Division for rearmament with the short Lee-Enfield rifle, in consequence of a high percentage of jams experienced with their Ross rifles during a hostile attack on May 1, 1916.
2.	I am accordingly of opinion that the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Divisions should be re-armed with the short Lee-Enfleld rifle. It will be remembered that the 1st Canadian Division was so re-armed on June 12, 1915.
3.	I am not in a position to effect this with the means at my disposal in France. I have' the honour to inquire therefore, whether the necessary number of rifles can be supplied from home sources, without interfering with, or delaying the arrival and arming of the divisions due from England and Egypt on which I am relying.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) D. Haig, General,
Commanding in Chief, British Armies in France.
[Sir Robert Borden. J
There is a further report from Sir Douglas Haig, dated June 21, 1916, which is also significant. It is addressed to the Secretary of the War Office in London, and reads as follows:
June 21, 1916.
Sir,-In reply to your No. 77/15/5307 (M.G.O.) of June 10, 1916, forwarding a copy of a telegram dated June 7, from the Governor General of Canada, I have the honour to inform you that the efficiency of the Ross rifle has been thoroughly tested by actual fighting in the field, and the application conveyed in my O.B./174 of May 28, 1916, was made after very cardful consideration of all the evidences available.
2.	I have again consulted the General Officer Commanding Second Army in case any fresh points have come to light during the recent heavy fighting by the Canadians near Ypres. He tells me that his experience of the working of the Ross rifle during the last fight has only confirmed him in his opinion that the Canadians, in the 3rd division at all events, have lost confidence in their rifle and he recommends that the rifles in this division be exchanged.
3.	Although the reports from the 2nd division are not to the same effect, I am of opinion that the Lee-Enfleld rifle should be issued to all three divisions of the Canadian Corps.
I must therefore adhere to my recommendation that the 2nd and 3rd Canadian divisions should be re-armed with the short Lee-Enfield rifle, and I would urge that the necessary steps to give effect thereto be taken without delay.
I have the honour to be.
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
D Haig, General,
Commanding in Chief, British Armies in France.
It is well to remember, in justice to the Ross Rifle Company, that Sir Douglas Haig states in his report that the opinion which seems to have been pretty general in the Third Division was not shared by the men of the Second Division; but he thought it desirable and wise to arm all three divisions with the Lee-Enfield, in order that all the British forces at the front should be equipped with the same rifle. On the 11th day of July the Secretary of State for the Colonies, in consequence of these reports, sent us the following telegram, addressed to the Governor General:
July 11. 1916
With reference to my telegram, June 10, report from General Offlcer Commanding in Chief in France has now been received by Army Council recommending that second and third Canadian divisions should be re-armed with short Lee-Enfleld rifles and Army Council have approved this. They hope to be able to utilize Ross rifles released and also those now in possession of Canadian troops in England for other purposes connected with the war, but ask that no more Ross rifles should be brought to England. Army Council will be responsible for supplying necessary rifles to Canadian troops on

arrival in England. If your Government desire to undertake manufacture of different rifles Suitable for use during war, Army Council think that rifles now being produced in America for British Army on lines of Lee-Enfield Mark III, but with improvements would be best.
Hon. members will observe that on the 26th of April, 1916, we had been informed that the British Government had no supply of rifles which would be available for rearming the Canadian troops. But conditions as regards supply and production evidently improved, because on the 11th day of July they entered into a clear and distinct engagement with us that they would hold themselves responsible for arming all the Canadian troops with the Lee-Enfield rifle, and they have carried out that engagement up to the present, and I have no doubt they will carry it out in the future. So that from the 11th day of July up to the present all the Canadian troops at the front have been armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle, and the British Government have undertaken on their part to see to it that all the Canadian troops sent to the front shall be armed with that rifle.
Might I ask why, after that date, the Fourth Division went over armed with the Ross rifle?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To which, on the 7th day of September, 1916, the following reply was received from Mr. Bonar Law in a cable message to the Governor General:
Tour telegram of the 31st Fourth Division were sent to France armed with Ross rifles, but I .ee-Lin fields have since been sent to France for purpose of re-arming. Re-arming should be completely performed by now.
From this I understand that although the Fourth Division went to France armed with the Ross rifle, the British Government, in pursuance of their engagement with us, ret-armed them with Lee-Enfield rifles before they were actually at the front.
That is the situation up to that time, the net result of it being this:	In the
summer of 1911, when the Canadian Government were made acquainted with the view of Sir John French that, for the reasons expressed in his report, it was advisable to re-arm the First Canadian Division with the Lee-Enfield rifle, we assented at once that this should be done, because it appeared that there had been jamming of the Ross rifle; that the ammunition was unsuitable; that the men had lost confidence in the rifle, and that a change was absolutely necessary. Then, having regard to the suggestion of Sir John French that the rifle might be made right by enlargement of the chamber; having regard to the fact that there was no other source from which rifles could be obtained; having regard also to the fact that, according to the best judgment we could procure, it would occupy at least a year before rifles of any other type could be turned out by the Ross company, we concluded, following the lines of Sir John French's suggestion, that the only course was to enlarge the chamber of the Ross rifle. Accordingly the Minister of Militia in, July, 1915, determined to enlarge it from .460 to .462, and in August, 1915, he determined still further to enlarge it to .464, with the expectation that the enlarged chamber would prevent jamming. When the question of further provision of rifles came rather urgently before us in the winter of 1916, after giving an order for
100,000	rifles with the enlarged chamber, we made inquiry of the British Government on the 30th day o'f May, 1916, whether out of the supply of rifles which they had ordered, it would ibe possible to supply Lee-Enfield rifles to us, and what number; and on the 26th of April, 1916, we received a reply that no rifles out of those ordered by them would be available for our use.
Later on, when further difficulty arose with regard to-the rifles, we sent a communication first to Sir Max Aitken and

afterwards to Sir William Robertson, suggesting that tests should be made, pointing out that according to our view the rifle was efficient if properly used, and desiring, after those tests had been made, that the result should be communicated to us. In June, 1916, we left the whole question of the re-arming of the Canadian troops at the front to the absolute judgment of the Chief of the Imperial General Staff and the Commander in Chief of ithe British army in the field; and when they determined, having regard to all consideration, that although some of the Canadian units were perfectly, satisfied with the Ross rifle, it would be advisable that all the forces should be re-armed we assented to that conclusion at once, accompanied as it was by the condition and undertaking that the British Government in the future would make themselves responsible for the arming of all the Canadian troops at the front with the Lee-Enfield rifle to which no exception seemed to have been taken, end in which at all events the troops seemed to have confidence, iso far as we could learn from the reports available.
Now, that is the situation as it presents itself to my mind. I have endeavoured to give the whole facts to the House so far as they can be disclosed with the consent of the War Office. My hon. friend, however, goes on and puts before us another question: What do we propose to do about the production of rifles in Canada? I want to point out in the first place that, so far as the arming of Canadian troops is concerned, we have the definite engagement of 'the British Government that our troops shall be armed, when, they go to the front, with the Lee-Enfield rifle. That engagement has been lived up to, as I understand it. For, although the Fourth. Division went to France armed with the Ross rifle, they were immediately afterwards armed with the Lee-Enfield, and are so armed today. The question of the production of rifles in Canada ceased to have the immediate urgency that it would have had if that engagement had not been given to us by the British Government. With this in mind, we come back to the question of what the Government has done with respect to the production of rifles in. this country in the future.
Certain negotiations are going on as to the disposition in Great Britain of our supply of Ross rifles, the most of which have been in use either by the British Government or ,by ourselves. We Tequire a considerable number in Canada of course for the

training of our own tro-ope-though I entirely agree that would be better, if it were possible, that out troops should be trained with the rifles they are to use at the front. In considering the question of what should be done, there are a couple of telegrams which have not yet been brought down 'and which it might be well that I should communicate to the House. In the telegram from which I am about to read there are some portions that, from considerations of public interest, I cannot disclose to the House:
Ottawa, September 5, 1916.
My advisers consider it important for purposes of common defence that adequate facilities for production of rifles should be maintained in Canada. They are impressed with the view that a standard rifle to be called Imperial Service Rifle should be adopted by Mother Country and all Dominions of Empire, if British Government can give them assurance that rifle known as Enfield .276 pattern adapted for .303 ammunition will be definitely adopted by British Government as standard service rifle my advisers would proceed to necessary examination for its adoption and preparation for adequate production here.' If on the other hand British Government have reached no definite conclusion as to type of rifle to be ultimately adopted my advisers would naturally desire to limit as far as possible expenditure for this purpose as it would have to be repeated in case another type should be adopted in early future. They would be grateful for full and prompt expression of views of His Majesty's Government as to situation which must be considered with regard to needs of whole Empire.
I havie stated that the date of that telegram is 5th September. In order to prevent ' misapprehension as to dates of telegrams, I may explain that when we send a telegram dated, for instance, 5th September, that telegram is received by the British Government on the 6th September. There i9 a difference of five hours in the time. Telegrams are thus referred to by the British authorities as of the following day- in the case I speak of this telegram is referred to as of 6th September. The reply is as follows:
Paraphrase of cypher telegram from Mr. Bonar Law to the Governor General.
London, September 19, 1916.
With reference to your telegram September 6th it is regretted by Army Council that it is impossible for them at present to give definite assurance as to the pattern of service rifle to be adopted after the war. Further experience may modify views now held, while the large stock of rifles which will have accumulated by the end of the war may render the adoption of any new pattern unlikely for some years to come. As regards the present manufacture of rifles suitable for use during the war the Army Council adhere to their opinion conveyed to you in the penultimate sentence of my telegram of July 11th.
Bonar Law.
As the telegram of July 11 may not be
clearly recalled by hon members, because of th.e mass of this correspondence,
I will refer to it again in order that the allusion in the document just quoted may be understood. The penultimate sentence of the telegram of July 11th is as follows:
If your Government undertake the manufacture of different rifles suitable for use during war. Army Council think that rifles now being produced in America for British Army on lines of Lee-Enfield Mark III, but with improvements would be best.
That is the same rifle described in a somewhat different way in my telegram of 5th Septembei In that telegram I referred to it as " the rifle known as Enfield, .276-pattem, adapted for .303 ammunition." I used that expression because I was informed by the Master General of the Ordnance that it would be understood by the Wiar Office, being the technical description of that rifle. I think it was in September, 1916, that we asked the Government to furnish us with a sealed pattern of that particular rifle in order that we might take steps, under the contract with the Ross Rifle Company, for its production in this country. On November 14 I made a recommendation to Council with regard to. it, and that recommendation was approved by His Excellency on November 15. It is proper that I should read that order in council, as it adopts for the purpose of future production in Canada the approved Lee-Enfield rifle which is being produced for the British Government in the United States, but which, as I understand, is not yet being produced in Great Britain, for the reason which I have already mentioned. The order in council is as follows:
November 15, 1916.
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report dated 14th November, 1916, from the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, stating that on the 27th day of March, 1902, His Majesty the King, represented by the Hon. F. W. Borden, then Minister of Militia and Defence, entered into an agreement with Sir Charles Ross, Bart., of Balnagowan, copy of which is appended, whereby the Government of Canada agreed with the said Sir Charles Ross to purchase from the said Charles Ross or his assigns all rifles required for the use of the Government. The said contract fixes no limit as to the time for which it shall remain in force.
That the said contract provided for the manufacture and delivery by the contractor in each year of such number of rifles not less than 10,000, as might be desired and signified by the Government in writing on or before the 30th day of September- of the year preceding the year in which delivery was to be made, each to correspond to a standard sample rifle to be provided by the said minister.
That the said contract further provided that should a new rifle be invented which the Gov-

ernment should desire to adopt or use the Government might furnish the contractor with a standard sample of such new rifle and give the contractor twelve months' notice in writing requiring that the rifles to be delivered by the contractor upon and after the expiration of the period of such last-mentioned notice should, correspond to the standard sample of such new rifle so furnished, the Government to protect the contractor against any actions for infringements of patents so far as such new rifles supplied to the Government were concerned, and upon and after the expiration of the said period all rifles to be delivered by the contractor should accordingly correspond to such substituted standard sample, and the contractor agreed to originally lay out and adapt his plant, machinery, etc., so as to provide the best facilities which could be reasonably foreseen to enable him to apply the same to the manufacture of any such new rifle which might so be desired.
That the said contract further provided for the fixing of the price to be paid for the rifles to be manufactured and delivered thereunder from time to time.
That from the date of the said contract all rifles required and used by the Government were, in accordance with the terms of the said contract, purchased from the contractor named therein, or from his assigns, the Ross Rifle Company, and the standard sample rifle furnished by the Minister of Militia and Defence as provided for in the said contract in 1902 with certain improvements and modifications made from time to time has been the rifle produced by the contractor up to the present time.
That much difference of opinion and much controversy has arisen as to the merits of the rifle so purchased and its usefulness as an active service weapon compared with other standard rifles adopted by the British Government. As a consequence repeated inquiries have been made and varying opinions given as to the desirability of substituting a new standard rifle for the rifle so manufactured. Concurrently with these inquiries, information was sought as to the possibility of procuring other standard rifles for the use of the Canadian forces. The readjustment of the contractor's factory for the production of a new standard rifle would involve great delay, and adequate provision for arming the Canadian forces in the meantime is necessary. Since the outbreak of war, however, the Government was not able, until very recently, to procure any other rifle in Great Britain or elsewhere for that purpose. On April 26, 1916, in response to an inquiry made on March 30, 1916, the Imperial Government stated that even up to June, 1917, there would be no surplus from British orders other than that already allotted to the Allied Governments, and that it was impossible to allocate from such orders any rifles to this Government. Early in July, however, the British Army Council, to whose decision the matter had been left by the Canadian Government, concluded that the Canadian Expeditionary Force should be armed with the Lee-Enfleld rifles, and the Army Council undertook to make themselves responsible for supplying the necessary rifles to the troops from Canada c n arrival in England. This arrangement was accepted, and it has been carried out. On the 5th September, 1916, the Imperial Government informed this Government that the condition indicated in their communication of the 26th April had changed, and

that it would be possible to arrange fer the transfer of a certain number of standard rifles to Canada from existing British orders.
Further correspondence took place with regard to the type of rifle which should be adopted in Canada. The Imperial Government, since the beginning of the war, has commenced, and is now carrying on the production of an improved rifle known as the Enfield 1914, or .276, adapted for .303 ammunition. The minister is informed that this rifle, as it is produced from time to time, will be issued by the Imperial Government to the British army, and the Army Council have advised that if this Government desire to undertake the manufacture of a new standard rifle the said improved rifle is considered the best.
In view, therefore, of the fact that other standard rifles are now available, the minister recommends that no further orders be given for the manufacture of the standard Ross rifle heretofore supplied to the Government under the said contract.
In view of the information obtained from the Army Council and of the very great desirability that the rifle to be issued to the Canadian forces should be the same in every respect as that to be supplied to the other forces of the British Empire, the minister further recommends that a new standard sample rifle be provided by the Minister of Militia and Defence, the same to be in every respect the rifle so to be supplied by the Imperial Government, namely, the Enfield, 1914, or .276, adapted for .303 ammunition, and be furnished to the contractor and his assignee, The Ross Rifle Company, in accordance with clause 6 of the said contract, and that the contractor and the said company be required, on and after the first day of December, 1917, to make all rifles supplied under the said contract to correspond to such last mentioned substituted standard sample rifle the Government undertaking to protect the contractor and his assignee against any actions for infringement of patents as stipulated by the contract, and, moreover, that the Minister of Militia and Defence be authorized to give a notice in the form hereto annexed to the said Sir Charles Ross and his assignee, The Ross Rifle Company.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
(Signed) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
It is necessary, for the purpose of giving the notice, referred to in the order in council, that it should be accompanied by the standard rifle itself. We were not able to procure a standard rifle in the time limited; therefore the order in council had to be amended as to the date at which t'he contractor should be called upon to undertake the production of the new standard rifle. As the new standard rifle was not supplied to us by the British Government until the 15th or 20th of January last, an amending order in council was passed by which the notice given to the contractor requires him to produce the new rifle on and after the 1st day of February, 1918, it being necessary under the terms .of the contract that he should have a year's notice.
The matter stands in that way at pre-

sent, and the question for the Government to determine is as to the extent of the order which should be given to the Ross Rifle Company for the improved rifle, or as to what other course, if any, the Government ought to take in the premises. On the one hand, we are confronted with the fact that after the conclusion of the war, we shall have, unless we dispose of them in the meantime, a very considerable number of Ross rifles, Mark III. I have spoken of some negotiations still pending with regard to disposing of some of these rifles. For the purpose of training under ordinary conditions of peace they would be useful to our troops, and it is quite possible that, under conditions of warfare different from those which have been encountered during the past two years, the Ross rifle might give perfect satisfaction. I am not prepared to pronounce an opinion upon* that, because there has been so much difference of opinion, so much controversy amongst experts, that it would be idle for me to venture on a subject which depends upon technical considerations as well as upon actual experience in the field.
The question, therefore, is under the consideration qf the Government at the present time, and we shall give our best attention to it. I should be very glad indeed if hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, who have taken an interest in this subject, and who are now fully seized of the situation as it presents itself to the Government, would be good enough to give us the benefit of their views, which, of course, will be most carefully and attentively considered. The situation is as I have described it. We have made provision, by arrangement .with the British Government, that our troops shall be armed at the front during the continuance of the war with a rifle to which no exception has been taken. We have the question as to whether anything can be done with the supply of Ross rifles which are not in use at the front; and, lastly, there is the question as to the extent upon which we shall enter upon the production of rifles of a new type. Hon. gentlemen who heard me read the telegram of the British Government dated 19th September will remember that they expressed a great doubt as to whether or not any rifle other than the improved Lee-Enfield rifle would be adopted as the standard service rifle in the immediate future, putting forward, as the reason for that view, the reasonable consideration that they would be in possession
of so enormous a supply of rifles after the war that they, would not care to embark upon the production of a new rifle upon the scale that would be necessary. The condition which confronts them confronts us in a smaller degree, because we shall have on hand, unless we dispose of them in the meantime, a very large number of Ross rifles, Mark III, at the conclusion of the war, more than will be ordinarily required by this country for several years to come under conditions of peace. In the meantime, the order which was given in February last to the Ross Rifle Company is being carried out, and the order which the British Government gave to^the Ross Rifle Company in the autumn of 1914 is also being carried out. Altogether the company has still to produce and deliver about
150,000	rifles, about 97,000 for us, I think, and about 57,000 for the British Government.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.

A unanimous opinion was expressed that the Canadian manufactured D.A.C. 1914 Mk. VII ammunition only, of those tried, was suitable for rapid fire with the Ross rifle, that provided a sufficient supply of Canadian manufactured ammunition of this type could be supplied, the other defects apparent were not sufficient to condemn the Ross rifle in view of the present shortage of rifles generally, and that those types of British made ammunition which were tried should not be issued to troops armed with the Ross rifle.
The committee were practically unanimous in advising that the Ross rifle should be employed on the lines of communication, and that if possible, the Canadian troops should be armed with the British rifle.

speechtext:
With regard to the following specific points which the committee were asked to answer, the questions and answers as st&ted below:
1.	There are frequent reports that the bolt action jambs after about 5 rounds.
2.	Full value of rapid fire cannot be developed unless:
(a)	Ammunition of Canadian manufacture is used.
(b)	Rifle is perfectly clean.
3.	That English made ammunition is slightly larger than Canadian eo that immediately the cartridge exploded the cartridge case fills the chamber so tightly as to cause a jamb.
4.	(a) That orders exist that on no account are troops to take out their magazine as it necessitates stripping the rifle.
(b) Unless the magazine is unloaded every 24 hours and the spring action eased, the magazine fails to respond.

6.	The screw of the bolt head expands under heat and renders it difficult to open the breech (presumably due to the number of bearing surfaces affected).
7.	The Ross rifle sight is defective because of its delicacy and the smallness of the figures which make it difficult ta adjust the sight easily.
8.	The magazine case is too thin and is dented easily. This causes a jamb as the spring cannot work.
9.	The foresight is not good for service work. The circular cover easily gets filled with mud and is difficult to clean.
10.	A hole has recently been bored in the base of the magazine to enable the cleaning of the magazine to be carried out with stripping the rifle.
11.	It is far easier to load the Lee-Enfield rifle than the Ross rifle with a clip of ammunition. A Lee-Enfield rifle takes 10 rounds a Ross 5 rounds.
12.	That the shape of the fore part of the chamber of the Ross rifle is different to that of the Lee-Enfield. That this does not allow of the same expansion' and is the cause of the jamb.
1.	Yes, but with British B. 1915 Mk. VII ammunition only.
2.	(a) Full value of rapid fire can be developed with ammunition of Canadian manufacture only.
(b) This point was not tested.
3.	The British made cartridge case appears to be of a slightly thicker gauge than that of Canadian manufacture and the diameter of the cartridge immediately under the rim appears to be slightly greater than that of Canadian manufactured ammunition. This may be the cause of jamming.
4.	(a) Yes.
(b) This possibly is the case but the committee were unable to test this point.
5.	This may be so, but the rifles were not tried under dirty condition.

speechtext:
I't should be noted that twenty-six Ross rifles per battalion are used in the Canadian forces at the front at present for sniping purposes, there being no question at all that for that purpose the Ross is superior to any other rifle known.
I do not know that I have emphasised sufficiently one point that ought to be borne in mind by every hon. member of the House, and by every one in this country who is disposed to consider in a reasonable way the situation that confronted this Government in the summer of 1915, after Sir John French's report had been received. I know, in a very intimate and confidential way, what the situation in regard to rifles was both for the British Government and certain others of the Allied Governments. The situation with regard to rifles, machine guns, 18-pounder field guns, howitzers and guns of larger calibre, such, as were being increasingly used in the field-the situation with regard to all these matters was detailed to me in a very frank way by the present Prime Minister of Great Britain two days before I left England in 1915. I cannot even at this date go into the particulars of the information Which he then afforded to me. But I do desire to emphasize to hon. gentlemen in this House that there was the most desperate and urgent need of rifles of any description in 1915. I could give the House, if it were permissible, information with regard to certain negotiations that were carried on in that year, in which our co-operation was asked for securing rifles of a somewhat antiquated type. The situation was not such as would justify the Government in considering a selection of rifles. The situation was one which demanded every possible effort that could be made in every direction to procure rifles of almost any description. Men were undergoing training'not only in this country but also in Great Britain, some without rifles at all and others with dummy rifles. The need was most intense, insistent and urgent. The Government could have the chamber of the Ross rifle enlarged, as the chamber of the Lee-Enfield had been enlarged, so that jamming would be prevented. What else could it do? I again point out that under the contract the Ross Rifle Company was entitled to one year before it could be called upon to produce rifles of a different type and that the British Government thought it could not be done in less than two years.
On the 21st of July, 1916, we requested the British Government to furnish the Boss

Rifle Company as soon as possible with all technical infornfation including drawings, specifications and samples of the new standard rifle to which I have alluded. We also inquired on that occasion as to whether or not the British Government proposed to continue their contract with the Ross Rifle Company for the Ross rifle, Mark III,-or whether they would require Ross to produce the new pattern of Lee-Enfield rifle under that contract. Various reminders were sent requesting a reply to that telegram, but none was received until the 28th of August, 1916, when the following reply was made:
With reference to your telegram of July 21, Army Council state that 'the improved pattern of Lee-Enfield rifle is not at present manufactured at Enfield, as considerable time would have been taken up in turning arms to new pattern. At present the new pattern is only made in America, and under the circumstances, the Army Council consider that there is no necessity for the Ross Company to communicate with Enfield.
There had been a suggestion in the previous telegram that the Ross Rifle Company should be put into direct communication with Enfield for this purpose. The telegram continues:
It is not considered possible by the Minister of Munitions to obtain delivery from the Ross rifle factory of the new pattern rifle in quantities under two years, but I am asking him to advise as to the best manner for the company to obtain the necessary specifications and drawings. I will telegraph as soon as possible as to the company's contract with His Majesty's Government
They supplemented that telegram on the 5th day of September, 1916, with this message:
With reference to my telegram August 28, position as regards contract for supply of 100,000 Ross rifles to His Majesty's Government is as follows: Ross rifles now being delivered though not authorized for service in the field are still of value for many purposes, training, arming home defence units, and arming marines. Therefore, immediate supply of these rifles of service. On the other hand it is not considered possible to obtain deliveries in large quantities of new pattern rifle from Ross factory in less than two years. At a certain date the supply of Enfield rifles will be more than sufficient for needs of British troops and all requirements of Allies will have been met. Minister of Munitions in these circumstances does not propose to modify contracts and so far as this contract is concerned could not agree to change of pattern. Minister of Munitions further suggests that if it is decided to change over factory to new pattern for manufacture for Canadian Government it will be very desirable from company's point of view, both as regards finance and shop organization to carry out contract with His Majesty's Government while plant is being changed over. On learning that it has been decided that company should take up

manufacture of new pattern rifle for Canadian Government, Minister of Munitions will render every assistance in his power; he will .give instructions that specifications and drawings be prepared in United States and will place representative of Ross company into communication with British experts who are watching manufacture in United States; further there is a certain amount of equipment (jigs and tools) accumulated rifle plant here and not now required ; if this can be adapted to Ross company's plant, Minister of Munitions will be glad to supply it to Canada. Suggested that representative of Ross company should examine this equipment with view of transfer.
Then there is a passage which I shall omit.
Will the Prime Minister state the date when the British Government will be able to take care of all their requirements?	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is precisely what I think it is not desirable to state.
Further on there is a telegram of the 11th of September which relates to the efforts of this Government to obtain a standard rifle of the type which the British Government advised us to manufacture. The members of the committee will bear in mind that we had already been informed that this rifle was not being manufactured in Great Britain and that it was being manufactured in the United States. Therefore, being desirous of obtaining it as soon as possible, if we-were going to adopt it as a standard, we started out on our own account to get necessary specimens of the rifle in order that we might take proceedings under the contract. But on the 11th day of September, 1916, we received this telegram:-
Stated by Minister of Munitions that Master General of Ordnance, Canada, has applied to Ministry Organizations of New York for a few serviceable rifles of new pattern. It is considered undesirable by minister to send any rifles not critically examined by Chief Inspector of Small Arms in this country, and he will therefore select five rifles jof pattern mentioned and despatch from here.
We did not receive those rifles until about the 20th day of January, 1917. I suppose they had to be sent from the United States to Great Britain, where they had to be critically examined by the Chibf Inspector of Small Arms, and thereafter they were despatched to this country, sealed and in the form which was necessary under the contract.
It was necessary for us, if we proposed to give an order for rifles of that type, not only to have tfie rifle itself, but to have the specifications and drawings; so we proceeded to take steps for the purpose of acquiring them. On the 19th day of November, 1916, not having received the drawings and specifications, this Government despatched to the Colonial Secretary a telegram in these terms:
Ottawa, November 19, 1916.
Your telegram September 5. Rifles. Specifications and drawings of Enfield rifle, 1914 pattern, urgently required before 1st December. Please telegraph probable date of arrival and also of shipment.
Devonshire.
And on the 19th November we sent this despatch:
Ottawa, November 19, 1916.
Your cypher telegram of 11th September last. Rifles. Urgently required for use as sealed patterns five Enfield rifles 1914 pattern. Hope this can be arranged and should be grateful to know by telegram date of shipment.
Devonshire.
On 12th December we received 'from the Colonial Secretary the following telegram addressed to the Governor General:
London, December 12, 1916.
With reference to your cypher telegram November 19, it is regretted by Minister of Munitions that he is not at present in a position to supply specifications and drawings of 1914 pattern Enfield rifle. No standard pattern of this, rifle has yet been definitely settled upon, as it has been found necessary for manufacturers to alter certain points in original design. With reference to the taking up of the manufacture of rifle Minister of Munitions wishes to give every assistance to your Government, and will give instructions that specifications and drawings should be prepared in America or this country as soon as all details of pattern are definitely settled, and as promised in my telegram of September 5, will place representatives of Ross Company in communication with British experts who are in United States watching manufacture of rifle.
Up to the present time the necessary specifications and drawings alluded t.o in these several telegrams have not been received. As I stated, we have received the pattern ,of the rifle itself, and, having that pattern, we have given notice to the Boss Bifle Company in accordance with the contract as already mentioned. But, as i am advised by the Department of Justice-by the Solicitor General who looked into the matter-that for an older under the contract it is necessary not only that we should have the rifle itself but that we should have the specifications and drawings which, as I have said, although asked for some months ago, have been delayed owing to the fact that the exact nature of these specifications and drawings had not been fully settled.

It may be that in these remarks, which have been somewhat extended owing to the necessity of Teading so many documents, I have overlooked some point suggested by hon. members on the other side, or it may be that some new point may be raised on which it would be proper to give information. I can only say in concluding my remarks, that if any further information is desired in any respect I shall be veTy happy to give it to the best of my ability. The Government ha3 absolutely nothing which it desires to conceal in connection with this matter, except so far as considerations of the public interest may make it undesirable to place certain communications or portions of communications before the House in such a way that the information will reach the enemy.
I submit to the House and to the country this correspondence, and this account of the conditions with which we have to deal, with a good deal of confidence that our course will be appreciated, as it must be if it is understood. Throughout we have been animated by one purpose alone, namely, that the gallant men overseas fighting in the Canadian forces should be equipped with an efficient rifle, and, more than that, a rifle in which they could have absolute , confidence. That has been the purpose, the desire, and the intention of the Government, and I think it is manifest from the correspondence I have read and the incidents I have described that the intention has been well carried out.

I think the House accepts the statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister in the spirit in which it is offered. We all realize that in a subject of such a confidential nature as this there is some correspondence which the right hon. gentleman could not produce to the House. It is very evident from the manner in which his statement has been made that some correspondence is withheld. For that reason it is not as easy to discuss the subject as if it were an ordinary business affair. Personally, I feel very grateful to the Prime Minister for the information he has given. If I can get just a few more questions answered along the same lines I shall be perfectly satisfied, or, at any rate, I shall not have much further to say. I should like to know whether, at any time after July 15, when it became evident that there was something wrong with the Ross rifle, any person in authority went to Sir Charles Ross, officially or unofficially, and asked him if he would manufacture a different type of rifle from the Ross rifle, and

if so whether he demanded a year's notice provided for in the contract, or whether he agreed to manufacture whatever kind of rifle the Government wanted. My reason for asking is found in the newspaper correspondence which took place last month. I have not it before me, but I read it as, I presume, the right hon. the Prime Minister did. We all know what that correspondence was. I think it began because of a statement made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) in Montreal. Sir Charles Ross, in his letter, stated in very plain language that he had always been willing to do whatever the Government wished him to do, that he had not stood on the letter of the contract but wished to carry it out in spirit, and had always been ready to make whatever changes and modifications the Government wanted to have made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of any person having called upon Sir Charles Ross to make such a proposal. I understand that he is under the impression that he spoke to me in 1915 with regard to approaching the British Government with a view to having all the contracts changed into a contract for the Lee-Enfield rifle, possibly to procure a larger contract from the British Government.
I have a good deal of confidential correspondence about some negotiations that he had concerning a proposed large contract with the Russian Government, in which he requested the assistance of the Canadian Government. I have no recollection of his having made that suggestion to me in 1915. If he made any such suggestion to- me as he thinks he did, it must have been of a casual character, because I 'have no recollection whatever of it. Further than that, I have had the correspondence examined and I find no reference in it to any such proposals. I am perfectly satisfied that the proposal is one which would not have been entertained by the British Government, for the reason that they have always adhered to the theory that it would be impossible for him to change his factory so as to produce a new rifle in quantities inside of about two years. I have read two telegrams which indicate that. Sir Charles Ross himself thinks that he would do it in a year, possibly in less than a year. We have to take into account, of course, the views of those whose experience in such matters would make their opinions valuable.	-

The Prime Minister
says that he will take the opinion of some

official in England in preference to the opinion of Sir Charles Ross. [DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not say
that. I said that in dealing with such a question we would have to take into account the view of experts, whether in .Great Britain or in our own department at home. We could not be absolutely sure that the view of the experts of the Ross Rifle Company woold be borne out in the end.

The Prime Minister has a great advantage in discussing this matter, because he has had an opportunity of taking it up, not only with the experts in Great Britain and in the department here, but also with Sir Charles Ross; whereas we on this side of the House have had no opportunity of discussing it with anybody. But it would seem to the ordinary observer that the man who has the most up-to-date rifle factory in America, and who has been able to turn out rifles at the rate of 1,000 a day, ought to have some idea as to how long it would take him to equip his factory. However, I have no knowledge of the matter; I simply accept the statement made by the Prime Minister. Has the Ross rifle factory during the last two years and a half been asked to make any changes in the rifle which they are manufacturing? If so, how many; and have they required a year's time within which to make the change, or have they done it in a much shorter time? If they have done it in a shorter time, how long has it taken to effect the changes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not want my hon. friend, or the members of the committee, or any one else to misunderstand me. I was not disparaging the ability or experience of Sir Charles Ross, for, as far as the mechanical details of the rifle are concerned, it is universally acknowledged that he is an exceedingly capable man. I only intended to suggest that a government, in the midst of a war, when the question of time is vital, must, in considering such a change, take into consideration the view which is entertained not only by the contractor, but also by their own experts and by the experts of Great Britain, whose experience and knowledge in such matters certainly should command respect. When the question of time is vital, one could not make a plunge into a proposal of that kind without taking the opinion of both sides into pretty careful account. My hon. friend asks me what changes have
been made. I have spent a good deal of time in endeavouring to get at the bottom of all these matters from first to last, and to see that the direction of events was in accordance with the best interests of our men at the front, but I certainly am not in a position to-night to give my hon. friend the information he asks, I should imagine that any changes, if any have been made, are of a very minor and trivial character, but I do not desire to commit myself to any statement on the subject unless I am absolutely sure that it is correct. I will get the information in written form from the Master-General of the Ordnance and give it to the committee to-morrow, or whenever the question is next taken up.

That is entirely satisfactory. I quite understand that the Prime Minister has had many things to take up his attention besides the matter of following up the changes that may 1 ave -taken place in the Ross rifle. Still, as he seems to have a very complete brief or the case, I thought he might possibly be able to tell us what changes, if any, have been made. There has been an enormous amount of talk throughout Canada during the last year in regard to the Ross rifle. We hear it stated in one place that the company must be allowed a year in which to make any change. I have been told by a member of the House since coming here that changes have been made inside of one or two months. I suppose they would be minor changes, but they would be changes just the same, and some alteration of the machinery would be necessary. I do not forget the fact that this country is at war, nor do I forget that up to a comparatively recent period the question of getting rifles of any kind was a very serious problem for Great Britain and her Allies-. But in the light of the report, which the right hon. gentleman has read to-night, of a committee appointed by General French away back in June, 1915, positively recommending that the Canadian troops at the front be not armed with the Ross rifle, it is most remarkable that the matter was allowed to drift along as it did. It could he justified only by the reason given by the Prime Minister to-night: that a rifle of almost any kind was better than no rifle at all. I do not think that the same charitable construction could be placed upon the actions of the Government after -the lamentable affairs of May, 1916, as could be placed upon their actions after the occurrences of 1915, because in 1916 the rifle

situation must have been, very materially improved. I quite appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister does not wish to state the date when the British Government expect to be entirely independent in the matter of the supply of rifles. He quite properly refused to give that information to-night, and I would suggest that he go over the remarks which he made this afternoon, because it is my impression that he gave that information, perhaps without realizing what he was doing. That was my reason for asking the question. However, in the months of June and July, 1916, the Government must have had some idea that the British Government were not in the straits that they had been in the matter of rifles. The best evidence of that is that on July 11, 1916, this Government was notified by the Secretary of State for the Colonies to send no more Boss rifles to England; that in future the British authorities would proviide the Canadian army with Lee-Enfields.
That is a fact which is plainly stated in the correspondence; therefore, there is no reason why we should not discuss it. We start out from the 11th day of July, 1916, with the fact that the British Government were able to furnish the Canadian Army with Lee-Enfield rifles and that they did not want any more Roes rifles brought to Great Britain. The question that occurs to the average business man is, why, if that condition of affairs existed, the Government have gone on manufacturing Boss rifles from the 11th of July to the present time, are asking this Parliament to vote $2,660,000 for the purpose of purchasing more Ross rifles, and are producing 80,000 more rifles which the British Government will not allow upon the firing line and do not want in England at all. I appreciate the fact that these Ross rifles would be useful for instructional purposes, and for drilling purposes; and, as the Prime Minister stated they might be used on the lines of communication, although I think not in France, for I cannot conceive that under present conditions they would be allowed there. But we must remember that at the lowest calculation there must be 100,000 more Ross rifles owned or controlled by the Government of Great Britain than possibly can be required for the troops now in Great Britain for instructional purposes, and it would seem to me that these 100,000 rifles could be brought to Canada. They would more than supply any troops that are in Canada or that are likely to be, for instruc-

tional purposes. Therefore, it would seem that if the British Government are furnishing and have been furnishing since July last, all the rifles that are used at the front, the supply of nearly 300,000 Ross rifles-it must be pretty near that number since we started, as 218,000 have been purchased- a supply of that kind, one would think, would be quite sufficient.
The first question I asked this afternoon I repeat now. Why, in view of this state of affairs, have the Government continued manufacturing the Ross rifle and why are they -spending so much money for an article which, according to all the evidence, is of no great practical use to Canada in winning this war. I know that the Prime Minister takes the ground that the Ross rifle factory could not be converted into a Lee-Enfield factory within two years. We have not any evidence upon that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did n.ot give any opinion of my own upon it.

The Prime Minister
gave the opinion of some one else, and I have no opinion upon it at all; therefore my opinion would not be as good as the Prime Minister's. But we must remember that we would not have to close down the Ross factory entirely in order to convert it into a factory for making another kind of rifle, for there is an enormous amount of machinery in a rifle factory that would apply to any kind of rifle. After all, about the only difference between the Ross rifle and the Lee-Enfield rifle is in the bolt chamber. All the machinery which would make the stocks, barrels, and bands, and the dozen odd parts of the rifle, would be applicable to another type. We have the evidence given by the Prime Minister himself that it would take only about $500,000 to build over the Ross rifle -factory into a Lee-Enfield factory, and that the British Government would agree to furnish the_ machinery, or a large part of it. That is stated in the communication which the Prime Minister has just read. With these facts in our minds, the thing which I cannot understand, and which, I think, will bother the people of this country, is why the Government have gone on since July, 1916, manufacturing this rifle, -and why they are still making it and purchasing 80,000 more when the Prime Minister himself stated this afternoon that after the month of July, 1916, the production of rifles was not a very serious matter. I think I am using almost the ex-act words which the Prime Minister

used. I think ihis first idea was that it was hardly worth while bothering their heads about a rifle until the war had ended, or at least until the Empire had decided upon the make of a rifle that would be Empirewide. There was a communication addressed to the War Office, I think in the month of September, 1916-I have forgotten the exact date, but I think it was in September-asking them if, in their opinion, it was worth while for the Canadian Government to enter into the manufacture of any kind of rifle until the matter had been decided by the Empire at large. The same answer came back that had been coming for four or five months; if you want to manufacture a rifle, take the American [DOT] 276. That seemed to be the answer every time. I appreciate the fact that my hon. friend has had some difficulty in getting the specifications and drawings, and, to some extent, in getting a' pattern rifle.

When my hon.
friend refers to the American -276 rifle, I suppose he means the British -276 made in the United States?

The Prime Minister has been speaking about that this afternoon, and I am only quoting his words. I mean the 1914 Enfield rifle manufactured in the United States. The same answer always came back, and it came back in this case: if you want to make a rifle, make the -276 according to the American pattern, It seems most remarkable that this thing was .allowed to dangle along for months, and that nothing had been done. Now we are down to the point that after the 1st day of February, 1918, the rifles supplied shall be according to this -276 or American Enfield. I do not know, but I would feel pretty badly to-night if I could bring myself to believe that we would require rifles in any quantity after February, 1918. It may be possible that we will require them, but I sincerely hope not. , It seems to me that, in that view of the case, it would be almost a useless expenditure of time and energy, let alone money.
I wish to call my right hon. friend's attention to just one other matter, and it is one which I cannot view in the same light as I have viewed the remainder of the statements which he made this afternoon and evening. It seemed to me that the principal reason given by the Prime Minister for continuing to manufacture the Ross rifle, and for the expenditure of $2,500,000 in the future on a weapon which
he himself must admit can be of no very great practical use as a military weapon, is that we are bound by the contract, and that we must carry out that contract. Why, Mr. Chairman, has the right hon. gentleman forgotten that this country is at war? Has he forgotten that you can break a contract, if it is necessary, under the War Measures Act? I do not care if there was no War Measures Act; surely if this nation has agreed with some one to purchase a rifle which is not of any good, we are not going to carry out the contract. I do not believe that we have reached that point. I do not believe that Sir Charles Ross would try to hold the Government for a moment to a contract of that kind. I believe that if the Government asked Sir Charles Ross tomorrow, or put him in the box before a committee of this House, he would tell them that not only is he willing now, but that he has been willing from the beginning to change that rifle to any pattern that the Government wanted. I believe that the Government could cancel that contract if they want to cancel it. I cannot for a moment conceive that any hon. man, with the nation at war, would try to hold the Government to the mere letter of a contract and say: because you have given me a contract to manufacture a certain article, therefore, I am going to have my pound of flesh, and I am going to demand that you carry out that contract to the letter. I would want some further evidence than that which has been produced to make me believe that. There is another thing which I cannot accept; nor do I believe that the Prime Minister himself can accept it or believe it possible, and that is that the Ross rifle factory would demand a full year's time in which to make a change in the class of a rifle.
As far as Sir Charles Ross is personally concerned, I have never seen him more than once or twice in my life, and I do not know anything about him at all, but I cannot conceive of any loyal, British subject standing on a condition of that kind, when the nation is at war, and saying: although I own the only rifle factory which we have in Canada, and notwithstanding the fact that you want these rifles changed in order that they may be of some benefit to this country in the prosecution of the war, I stand on my legal rights and I will not make that change within twelve months. If I were the Prime Minister and a contractor should take that ground, it would not take me very long to put another

man into that factory who would carry out any changes that the nation wanted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by that? How could we put another man in charge?

Do you mean to say
that if there is a rifle factory in charge of a man who says that he will not make such a change within a year simply because the contract says he does not have to, that you could not take that factory rover and put somebody else in charge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do you mean to expropriate it?

Take it; I do not care what you call it. I would take it and so quickly that he w.ould never know what had happened to him. I do not think that I have to argue that before the Prime Minister. I do not believe that condition of affairs exists at all, and I think the Prime Minister would be much happier arguing that possibly it could not be done than that as he says because of the contract he could not do as he wished to do. However we have the explanation from the Prime Minister. I am very glad that the country has it and I think it would have been more fitting if we had had the facts laid before the public long ago. I realize that much of what has come put to-day has transpired since Parliament adjourned in May last, but there was a good deal which could have been given to the country a year ago. However, the country now has the information. I, for one, still hope that the Government will reconsider the matter and attempt to bring about the manufacture of rifles in Canada. As I said this afternoon, I agreed with that principle in 1904 and I agree with that principle to-day. I do not see any reason why rifles cannot be manufactured in Canada as well as in any other place in the world. I know they can be manufactured because they are being . manufactured. A rifle which for sniping purposes, as the Prime Minister admits, is the best rifle in the world, is being made to-day. As he says, this is the best equipped factory on the continent and therefore there is no reason why this factory could not be kept in existence and why they cannot accept the offer of the British Government and convert it into a Lee-Enfield factory. Notwithstanding the opinion of the Prime Minister, I do not think there is any reason why this factory could not, within a reasonably short time, be turning out Lee-Enfield rifles, which we know would be of
fMr. Carvell.l
some benefit in winning this war, instead of spending a year's time and $2,500,000 in turning out a rifle which, I am afraid, will not be of very much value to the Empire and which, the British Government do not want at all. I place this view before the Prime Minister, but I do not do so in a controversial spirit. I have tried to discuss the facts, and I do think that even at this late date there is time for the Government to do better than they have done and get much better results for the country than this proposal which they put forward would give.	,
Just another word and that is to the contractual part of the matter. The Prime Minister tries to make it appear that because this contract was in a sense perpetual they were compelled to go on and manufacture Ross rifles or rifles of some kind. The argument I used a few moments ago applies to this as well. If this country is at war and wants rifles or munitions or materials of any kind, all it has to do is to say so. It may be a question of adjustment later on, there may be some damages to pay, but that is a pretty lame excuse for manufacturing something that this country does not require, that is of no benefit to the country and which does not make for munitions necessary to the winning of the war. There is not much use in notifying the Ross Rifle Company that all rifles to be furnished by them after the first of February, 1918, must be of a certain pattern.
