Unless the Government makes with the company a contract sufficiently large to make it of some value, there is no object in going on and manufacturing. If you take, say, 12,000 rifles for this year, which, as I understand, is the minimum amount which the Government must take, at $30 apiece, and I believe that is the price for the rifle and the bayonet, that is only $360,000. That is th^ total cost of the 12,000 rifles. According to the information received this afternoon, it will cost $500,000 to equip the factory so that unless the Government go into this-
How much did the hon. gentleman say it would cost to equip the factory?
About half a million.
For what?

For re-equipping the
factory.
That is only for the change in the gauges.

That is all. The major
portion of the factory - would be equally suited to the manufacturing of the Lee-En-fields a-s the Ross. But there was the statement made this afternoon by the Prime Minister that the factory could be converted into a Lee-Enfield' factory for about half a million dollars. If you stand by the letter of the old contract, which means that the company must manufacture, say, 12,000 rifles, which the .Government take at $30 apiece, that amounts only to $360,000 while it whuld cost half a million dollars to change the factory over. That means that the contractor will not carry out the work and you will be doing nothing. If you follow out that contract to its logical conclusion, it means that the factory is closed down. I do not believe that it is in the best interests of Canada, of the militia of Canada, or of the British Empire, that the Ross rifle factory, or any other factory, that can manufacture rifles or anything else that is required for the conduct of the war should be closed down. I can only conclude by expressing the hope that the Government will reconsider this matter and put all the energy which they can into it, accept the offer of the British Government for these jigs and tools, equip the Ross rifle factory and manufacture something which will be of assistance to Canada and the Empire in the winning of the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is exactly what we have asked them to do in this order in council whidh I have read. The hon. gentleman seems to regard the Ross rifle as a particularly fragile article. I do not so regard it at -all. The Ross rifle has a more delicate mechanism, it is admittedly a better target rifle, tout when it was subjected to the test under conditions of war which prevailed during the past year or two

Did my right hon,
friend say it bad -a more delicate mechanism?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought so.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I bow to the
superior knowledge of my hon. friend but I have so understood it from certain authorities which may not be so convincing on the subject as my hon. friend's opinion. But, I think I could give him some testimony to that effect. The despatch from the British Government to which I have alluded states that for certain purposes,
although not for service in the field, the Ross rifle is valuable, such as the training of the army, and so on. After grave consideration of the matter we gave this order in February last just as the British Government had given their order in the autumn of 1914. They are continuing their order. They are bound by the contract to have it fulfilled and pay for the rifles on delivery. We gave an order in February 1916, and we are bound by the terms of the contract. We must fulfil the contract and we must pay for the rifles. Sir Charles Ross has accomplished very great things in equipping bis rifle factory for war purposes. I would not be disposed to treat him in any harsh or unfair way, and I think when my hon. friend suggests that we should take him by the coat collar and put him out of the factory if he did not do this, that, or the other thing which he was not obliged to do under the contract, he is asking us to adopt a course which would hardly be consistent with fair play. I think it would be unfair not to have regard to the very large expenditure which Sir Charles Ross has made for the purpose of turning out rifles which were of a type approved by the late Administration, and approved also by the present Administration. My hon. friend might realize also that the 1914 Enfield rifle, according to the view of the British Government expressed in the telegrams which I have read, is a better rifle than that which is at present being manufactured in Great Britain. Nevertheless "they have not attempted to manufacture that model in Great Britain up to the present time, and that obviously for the reason I have already suggested.
Have they accepted any from the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know.
None whatever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that they have accepted any; I do not know that they have not. I would suppose that the reasox they have carried on the manufacture in the United States, and not in Great Britain, is that in the United States it was necessary to build up a new organization, and therefore that new organization could be built up for the purpose of producing a new rifle, whereas in Great Britain they had their plants and factories all ready for the manufacture of the previous type of Lee-Enfield, and they carried on with that, because to have



attempted to make a change in Great Britain would have involved an unfortunate and unjustifiable delay.
My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) says that rifles produced after the 1st of February, 1918, may be of no use in this war. That is perfectly true. The war may have ended by that time, and in the way we all hope it will end. But it might also have been in my hon. friend's mind, or in the mind of any reasonable person, in July or August of 1916, that rifles produced after the 1st of September, 1917, would not be of any use in this war; and the outcome of the war may still be such as would justify that anticipation. So it is perfectly idle to suggest that the Government could have taken any other course than that which they did take under the oircumstarmes. My hon. friend has referred to the condition of the Ross rifle in Great Britain, and suggested that the rifles might be brought back, and the present contract cancelled. As I have already explained, there are some negotiations on foot in regard to the Ross rifle in Great Britain, and possibly some announcement may be made to the House later in the session as to the outcome of these negotiations.

Would' the right hon.
gentleman let me know whether he found out during the dinner hour who it was that ordered or was responsible for the reduction of the chamber of the Ross rifle from .462 to .457 in 1910? v

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I stated at the time that my information did not come from the Department of Militia and Defence, but that it waS reliable. I have asked the deputy minister to procure absolutely accurate information on that point, which I shall give to the committee.

I understand that
it was on the recommendation of Colonel Harkom, the expert adviser ito the Militia Department under;. Sir Frederick Borden. The Standing Committee on Small Arms was never consulted. A mistake arose in this way. The Lee-Enfield rifle for the proof charge had exactly the same chamber as the Ross rifle for the finished charge. I forget the figures, but they are all on Hansard. The proof charge of the Lee-Enfield was, I think, about twenty some odd tons. Then the rifle was fired in proof, the expansion being greater than the tensile strength of the steel, the [DOT]chamber of the Lee-Enfield rifle was expanded about two-thousandths of an inch. The tensile strength was from forty-eight to fifty-two

thousand-fifty-two thousand being the proof charge. The steel after expanding did not contract back to the primary size of the chamber. With the Ross rifle, the proof charge was the same: fifty-two thousand or thereabouts, but the tensile strength of the Ross was from eighty to one hundred thousand pounds to the square inch., and accordingly there was no expansion in the chamber of the Ross; it remained exactly as it was. The chamber of the, Ross rifle was therefore the size of the proof charge, two thousandths of an inch less than the chamber of the Lee-Enfield. That was remedied in England and France. I do not want to take any part in this discussion, as I understand it is all about the contract.
The chamber of the Ross rifle was, of course, changed a couple of years ago, but let us take the Ross rifle with the small chamber. I did not h,ear the reports that were read this afternoon, nor have I seen them, but I challenge the world to produce a report showing a test between the Ross rifle with the small chamber, and the Lee-Enfield, with good ammunition for both rifles, where the Ross has not beaten the Lee Enfield. I go further and take dirt mud, and sand tests, of which we have had scores officially and otherwise, and I challenge any man to produce a report of what we call these official tests, even with the small chamber in the Ross, where the Ross rifle has not beaten the Lee-Enfield. I go further and say that even with defective ammunition, which has been the cause of all this trouble-it was not the rifles at all but the defective ammunition with the soft cartridge case-I will not say that the Lee-Enfield has not stood the fire as well as the small chambered Ross, but I say they are about even. But since we enlarged the chamber of the Ross rifle, I challenge any one to show a report of any tests here or in the British Army, where the Ross rifle, even firing bad ammunition, has not done infinitely better than the Lee-Enfield.
Was the hon. gentleman present after eight o'clock when the Premier read a report of the committee appointed by Sir John French in the month of June, 1915?

The Ross chamber was not enlarged then. I care not what the report is. There is no such, test report in existence that has been made as between the two rifles where the Rose did not beat the Lee-Enfield. I know what has been done. '
The Premier read it.
He did not read a comparative test between the two rifles.
Yes, he did.
I should like to see it. I say that such a test was never made -by Sir John French. A hearsay report was ,made by one of his officers, but no comparative test.
If the report is produced, what will the hon. gentleman say?

It cannot be produced for no comparative tests were made there by any authority whatsoever. I saw one report in a Canadian paper of a test between the two rifles that never occurred. One day they were illustrating to General Carson and Sir Max Aitken the defective cartridges. They took a boy, who was an engine driver and who had never fired more than twenty shots out of a Ross rifle in his life, to handle the Ross rifle, putting him in competition with an expert artillery man who was using the other rifle. As soon as a competent man was put on to handle the Ross rifle, with the defective cartridges it was found that the Lee-Enficld jammed more quickly than the Ross.
That is not the comparative test referred to' by the Prime Minister this evening.
I do'not know to what the right hon. gentleman referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was some test referred to in Sir John French's report made on the 5th of June, 1915.

There was no
such test for mud and dirt and all that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say it was for mud or dirt; it was for defect in jamming.

That is the point I am making. The. jamming was due to defective ammunition. I had the reports and I presume they should be in the department. I do not know whether they have been read here tonight or not. There was a report of the 28th Regiment of Regina having a mine exploded in front of them and in their attempt to take the trench, twelve of the rifles jammed. The cry immediately went up "Ross rifles jamming." Col. Embury knew from experience that it
27*
was the ammunition that was bad because they had been trained in England not to use certain brands-of ammunition; but in spite of all the orders that this ammunition was not to be served out to the Canadian troops, it was found bad mixed with good in every regiment that had the Ross rifle and it was not found in a solitary regiment that had the Lee-Enfield rifle. Five thousand rounds of defective ammunition were found in the pouches of one particular regiment after the fighting was over,
Was it a German conspiracy ?

I do not know; I was not there. The men were disgusted with the rifle, the consequence being that Colonel Embury took the twelve men with the Lee-Enfield rifle and twelve men with the Ross rifle and made them test their rifles with the defective ammunition, and every man was convinced that defective ammunition jammed in the Lee-Enfield rifle after fifteen or twenty rounds had been fired, and in the Ross rifle only after fifty or sixty rounds had been fired. The Lee-Enfield rifle was put out of action after seventy-five or ninety rounds had been fired, and the Ross rifle only after a hundred to a hundred and twenty-five rounds had been fired. In every instance the Ross rifle proved better than the Lee-Enfield with defective ammunition, but with good ammunition neither rifle jammed, and they could not possibly jam. I could produce officers who are in the city to-night who fought with the Princess Patricias, with the Munster Fusiliers, with the Guards, with practically every British regiment- there are none in the city who fought with the Gordons-and they know that it was the defective ammunition that caused the jamming. There were three brands of it. Soft shells or soft cartridge cases would glue to the sides of the chamber and could not readily be extracted; but the tests are in the department and can be produced, if that has not already been done, showing where in England, France and Belgium these tests were made, and in every solitary instance with good ammunition there was no trouble with either rifle. With the defective ammunition, the Ross rifle would sometimes jam, but always later than the Lee-Enfield, the fault being entirely due to the ammunition. Although the British forces did not seem to be aware of it early in the war, they are aware of it now. The Canadian forces were not aware of it. At

the battle of St. Julien and the second battle of Ypres, a great deal of the ammunition the boys carried was Canadian ammunition that was absolutely perfect, and there was not one case*of jamming except where defective ammunition was .served opt to one of the brigades.
The Third Brigade?

No, I think it was the brigade under General Currie. The only thing the Canadians had to defend themselves with, with the exception of a few machine guns, was the Ross rifle, whereas the Germans had rifles, machine guns by the hundred and also their artillery and aeroplanes flying over our troops, and yet the Ross rifle firing the good Canadian ammunition carried our soldiers right through. The next day or two after the first three days of the fighting the Durhams and the Yorks were brought up to fill up the gaps on the right of the Third Brigade. When they began to fire with the defective ammunition, they found they could not Ato their rifles and many of them were shot down. They threw away their rifles and did the only thing they could do- fell back; they had no other recourse than to retire. Some of our rifles firing the bad English ammunition also jammed and there was considerable trouble, all due to the ammunition. Neither the Lee-Enfield nor the Ross rifle has jammed with good ammunition. Those who are familiar with rifles know the sand and mud test, of getting the rifles - and ammunition all dirty and testing them out. Where such tests have been made, with good ammunition or bad ammunition, the Ross rifle with the large chamber has beaten the Lee-Enfield.
Then why was the Ross rifle condemned?

I did not condemn it. You had better ask those who did. It has been pointed out that the Ross rifle is longer than the Lee-Enfield. The Ross r.fle is practically the same length as the Mauser rifle and it is the standard length. For trench warfare, of course, it is handier to have a short rifle. The only objection General Turner told me he could find to the Ross rifle was its length. When I pointed out that it was the same length as the Mauser rifle, he said that the soldiers had got the idea that the Lee-Enfield rifle was handier for running through a trench at night. That may have been true, but all that is done away with. Those who

make raids on the trenches use bombs and revolvers; only the men who stand out on top of the trenches use rifles. General Turner told me last summer and also previously that the Ross rifle was a little long for work in the trenches. When the decision came this year to change the rifle,' I spoke to General Byng about it. The Prime Minister offered to have a competitive test, if I remember aright. I presume it has been produced to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Why was that test not held, may I ask? It was because everyone on either side knew that there would be bnly one result. We had scores of tests in England and. in France, and they knew that if a comparative test was made with good ammunition, the Ross 'rifle would come out on top for mud tests, and they knew that if there was a comparative test for bad ammunition-and we have had them again and again for each rifle in such a way that no favouritism was shown -the Ross rifle would always stand up a little better than the Lee-Enfield.
I have made no fuss about it, because the rifle was gone, and I felt that many of the boys were honestly uncertain about the rifle from the attacks made upon it, and many others were made uncertain. I would say: Don't carry a rifle that you have not confidence fn, but if you feel that way about it, change it. It was on that ground that General Byng advocated the change. He said he did not know the merits or demerits of the rifle, but the story was abroad that the Ross rifle jammed. A number of the English soldiers got the idea that our rifles were not what they ought to be, and a lot of Canadians got the idea that maybe our rifle was not as good as the English rifle. Another point. I have reports here, but I do not wish to bother the House with them-for the thing is past-showing the action of some of the regiments when they were ordered to give up the Ross rifle and take the Lee-Enfield. I might mention one case. Colonel Rose, of the Welland regiment, as well as others, entered a most determined protest. He said that he had tried again and again to make scores with the Lee-Enfield without success, but with the Ross rifle the score was 75 per cent for the entire regiment at 600 yards down to 100 yards rapid fire. And that is the sort of shooting that made the Germans hesitate at St. Julien, and caused them to believe that the Canadians were armed with

machine guns. With the Lee-Enfield tried over and over again, Col. Rose's regiment had only been able to make a score of 29 per cent for the whole regiment. He declared that it meant murder to change the rifles; one man with a Ross rifle was equal to two men with the Lee-Enfield, the shooting was so rapid and so accurate, and the sighting so easy. I say I have reports to this effect, but I have not bothered to give them, for the thing has gone by, so let it go.

While we are cleaning up things and getting information, would the hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) tell us what took place about the bolt of the Ross rifle? I have seen reference to the fact that enormous sums of money were spent

Not much money. Well, there was a good deal of it, too. The cam action of the bolt depends upon the lugs, as they are called. These lugs were made soft so that they would stand the recoil without breaking. They were tempered to just the proper consistency. Somebody conceived the idea that these should be hardened, and this was done in the case of a number of the rifles. By whose authority this was done, I do- not know, but I believe it was that of some officers at the camp in Kent. We sent over three thousand bolts properly tempered. But these people hardened them again, as we found out afterwards.
What was the result?
They were made as brittle as a piece of glass, almost; the bolts were practically ruined. It was a piece of meddling on the part of somebody-on whose part I never found out.
Was this hardening process carried out under instructions of the Canadian Government?

No, we gave no instructions on the subject. I asked half a dozen times, but did not find out definitely on whose authority the thing was done. I heard a variety of stories about it, but I do not wish to mention any names when I am not sure of the facts. It was not done by authority of General Carson. He heard of it and was informed that it was necessary.
Is it true that over 100,000 rifles were so treated?
I never heard it said that there were that manv.
1 have heard all sorts of stories about it-that there were from 75,000 to 150,000 rifles so treated.
I never heard that there were as many as that. The number, as I was informed, was several thousands.

If the committee and the people of this country could reconcile, in the first place, the opposing positions taken with reference to making a change in the Ross rifle by two members of the Government, and, in the second place, the opposing positions taken by Sir Charles Ross, the contractor, as against both of these gentlemen, the explanation which was given here as to the change would be the more readily accepted. As I understand the right hon. Prime Minister-and his explanation seemed reasonable-the chief objection to making the change was the time that would be consumed in carrying it out. But, speaking in Montreal in December last, the hon. the Solicitor General explained tnat the difficulty which confronted the Government in this regard was that the Government was bound by the contract made with the former Administration, and being so bound couid not make a change. Here are two different positions taken by these two distinguished gentlemen. As against both of them, Sir Charles Ross, in his letter to the Ottawa Citizen of 12th January, 1917, takes an entirely different position. In the first place, he does not seem to regard time as an element containing any difficulty whatever in making the change, and in the second place he makes it quite plain that if at any time the Government desired to make a change his company would not seek to hold them to the terms of the original contract. So that there may be no doubt on this point, let me refer the committee to that letter:-
You ask whether I made it clear to the Government at any time after the outbreak of war that the Ross Rifle Company would be willing not to stand on the letter of the contract or if Mr. Meighen was right in affirming at Montreal that the Government was "bound" by the contract made by the late Administration.
I am quite willing to reply to your question but to enable me to select the most appropriate extracts from official documents to back up my statement, I should like to know authoritatively, first, just what Mr. Meighen means by the word "bound."
Does he mean to repeat the historical platitude that Governments of Canada keep faith and are as a result bound by agreements made by themselves or their predecessors? Or does he allege that the Government because it was "bound" -was, as a result, hampered and prevented from taking the best course in the gen-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have placed the contract in the pages of Hansard to speak for itself. It is obvious that the terms of the contract cannot be modified by a letter written to a newspaper. Sir Charles Ross since the outbreak of the war has used every effort to turn out in the greatest possible numbers and with the least possible delay the rifles which have been ordered by the Government. I have already given him credit for the enterprise, promptness and vigour with which he undertook to discharge that very important task. I am not aware that the terms of the contract have otherwise been modified in any way. However, II will make inquiry and see whether there is any document on record indicating that it was the intention to depart from the terms of the contract as I have placed it before the committee and as it is now in Hansard.

A few minutes ago the ex-Minister of Militia made a somewhat re-^ markable statement. He said that the bolts' of thousands of rifles had been hardened, so that the lug holding the bolt in position became as brittle as a piece of glass, broke off and in many cases flew put in the men's faces. Certainly there is something about the treatment of these bolts which the country does not know. I know the ex-Minister fairly well; when he skates over a thing like he did over this matter to-night, I always get suspicious. I wish that the Prime Minister, who does not skate, wpuld investigate this matter and give the commit-

tee some information when the subject comes up again for discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Probably some information can be obtained on the subject. As I have already said, we have nothing to conceal about this matter; if a mistake has been made in dealing with the bolts it is proper that the committee should be informed of it. I shall be very glad when this matter is taken up in committee again, to give any information that may be available on the subject.

' On the 9th of December the new Minister of Inland Revenue, on his arrival at Quebec the day after he had been sworn in, declared in the presence of a large number of the workmen employed by the Ross rifle factory that he was authorized by his colleagues to state that the removal of the factory from Quebec had never been contemplated and that the factory would remain where it was. Probably the rumour to that effect had been started" by the announcement that the construction of a- new Dominion arsenal in Lindsay, Ontario, had been commenced. What is the policy of the Government regarding the manufacture of munitions and the manufacture of rifles in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue asked me before he went to Quebec whether it was the intention of the Government to remove the Dominion Arsenal from Quebec. I told him that that had not been contemplated, and that it was not the intention of the Government to remove the Dominion Arsenal from Quebec.
What about the Ross rifle factory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He asked me
whether there was any intention of doing away with the Ross rifle factory or of removing it from Quebec. I told him that that had not been in contemplation, and that it was not the intention of the Government to remove it. I understand that the declaration which the Minister of Inland Revenue made is in accordance with that.

What is in contemplation with respect to the arsenal at Lindsay? If my memory serves me correctly, the late. Minister of Militia said that Quebec was not a very safe place in which to manufacture munitions-that it was deemed advisable to manufacture munitions on a larger scale at a point more inland.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN. I do not understand how my hon. friend can find anything

inconsistent in the two statements. An arsenal has been established at Lindsay, from which ammunition is now being turned out. It is quite consistent with that that the Dominion Arsenal at Quebec, which has produced ammunition in small quantities in the past, should be continued.
Is there any provision in this contract with the Ross Rifle Company which gives the company the exclusive right to manufacture rifles for or supply rifles to the Government of Canada9

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Ye3, the Government are bound to purchase from that company all the rifles that they require, and they are bound also to purchase from them not less than 10,000 rifles every year. I have not the contract before me-it has been sent to Hansard-but, as I recall it, the only qualification is that if the Government, in case of war or emergency, calls upon the company to produce rifles in very large numbers and the company in reply notify the Government that they can produce only a certain smaller number, then the Government would be at liberty to obtain the additional number wherever they might be available.
Has the Prime Minister any information as to what the cost of the Ross rifle establishment was at the outbreak of war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I could not tell my hon. friend just what it was at that time, or, indeed, what it is at present. I know that the factory has been very considerably enlarged by the addition of units, as they call them, since the outbreak of war. It is only in that way that the company has been enabled to produce a greatly increased quantity of rifles during the past two and a half years.

There is, then, a provision that in case of war, such as did take place, if the company was not able to meet any demand made by the Government, the Government could take other means to meet that demand?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, if it could get the rifles anywhere else. The situation that presented itself to the Government was that we could not get them anywhere else; therefore, we simply had to ask the Ross Rifle Company to do the best that they could. Their best was really beyond the anticipation of any person who knew what their resources were when war broke out.
What was the eapacity of their factory in 1914?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Deputy Minister of Militia informs me that at the outbreak of war their maximum output was
20,000	a year.

I understand the Prime Minister to say that under the contract the Ross Company would be obliged to manufacture any pattern of rifle which the Government would require, the Government being bound to purchase at least 10,000 per year. If the Ross Company were required by the Government to make the necessary changes in plant in order to manufacture the Lee-Enfield instead of the Ross, which would entail a large initial capital expenditure, is the Government supposed to repay to the company part of that capital investment? Would it be fair to expect the Ross Rifle Company to make the necessary changes upon a small order of say 10,000 per year? It seems to me that that would hardly be a fair way of dealing with the company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate what my hon. friend says. Of course, we do not intend to take any course which might be regarded as unfair to the company, especially having regard to the great vigour and resourcefulness which the company displayed in increasing its output. I agree entirely with my hon. friend that, possibly, if the contract was strictly enforced in that respect, a result that would not be regarded as quite fair to the company might follow. That is one of the difficulties of the situation which confronts the Government at the present time. We must take into account, on the one hand, the fact that we may have a very large number of Ross rifles, already manufactured, which would be sufficient and well adapted for the training of our troops in time of peace, a larger number probably than would be required in time of peace for that purpose. On the other hand, we have to take into account the fact that it is not advisable, as has been urged by the hon. member for Carleton, to continue the production of the Ross rifle Mark III. Therefore, we have directed the company, by notice under the terms of the contract, to manufacture the Enfield rifle of 1914, adapted for .303 ammunition. So that on the one hand, there is the fact, which faces the Government of the United Kingdom as well, that there will be this large surplus of rifles. On

the other hand, there is the consideration pointed out by my colleague from Halifax (Xvlr. Maclean) Inal if we followed out the strict terms of the contract, and simply ordered 10,000 rifles of the new type, the company might be put to an expense for the change of gauges, and for different plant and machinery, which would be greatly in excess of the order for the first year, and might probably equal the price to be paid for two years' orders if they should be restricted to the minimum fixed in the contract. I can only say- that we must take all these considerations into account, and that we have no disposition to act in a manner that might be regarded as unfair or harsh towards the Ross Rifle Company. I say that for the -reason that I think they have done remarkably well in increasing the output as they -have done since the war. began.

If the contractors are obliged to make the change in August, 1918, any arrangements to be made between the Government and the contractors should not be left until too -late a period. Of course that is quite obvious.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate that.
- Mr. CARVELL: I cannot understand the pessimism of my right lion, friend over the possibilities of making rifles in Canada. It seems to me that we have had an object lesson in Canada during the last two and a half years that ought to lessen all the pessimism-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is the
pessimism alluded to?

About the possibility of converting the Ross factory inside of two years in order to make rifles of a new type. He has given us a statement by some official in England who 'has some doubts about our ability to convert this factory in two years. I would like to carry him back to -the time, a little over two years ago, when the same authorities in England cabled over here to know if it would be possible to get 200,000 rounds of shrapnel in America, not in Canada, but in America, -and when the ex-Minister of Militia cabled back that he thought they could fill the order in Canada, and they went to work upon it. The ex-Minister of Militia himself stated the qther day that $700,000,000 had been expended in Canada by the British Government in the manufacture of munitions during the past two years. The same people who did not

believe that shrapnel shells could be made in America two years ago, who wondered if 200,000 rounds could be made in America, possibly honestly believe that you cannot change this rifle factory to enable it to manufacture Lee-Enfields within two years; but if our experience of munition work in the past two years is any criterion as to our abilities, I think that that man, whoever he may be, is incompetent, and that my right hon. friend is deserving of the severest castigation for listening to his opinion. I think he ought to have more faith and more optimism in this country than he has. If he had one-quarter or one-half of the optimism he ought to have, he would not see any lions in his path; he would go on and ask the manufacturers to make these rifles in the way they ought to be made to enable us to do our duty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad to find that my hon. friend is converted to an entirely new view as to the possibilities of manufacturing in Canada.
Oh, no, I have not changed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is now paying a remarkable tribute to the work of the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence, and to the work of the committee which he organized. It shows a comprehension long delayed on the part of my hon. friend which, I am sure, is an earnest of still better things to come. I should like to point out, however, that the manufacturers of Canada themselves were not very sure about their ability to do anything like what they have done when the proposal was first put before them. We have the testimony of the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence that he found a great deal of difficulty in inducing manufacturers in Canada to undertake the work at first, and that it was only some of them who were willing to undertake it. I am not at -all disposed to minimize the resourcefulness and ability of the Canadian people. I do know, however, that there has been, and still is, under present conditions, a good deal of difficulty about getting the plant and machinery of the type alluded to. At least, I have been told that by those who ought to know. But. when my hon. friend suggests that he is a better authority as to the time requisite for this purpose than the men who have been devoting their lives to work of this kind-
I did not say that I knew; I said, I would take the opinion of the man who was doing the manufacturing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is where I would differ from my hon. friend. I would not necessarily take the opinion of either of two persons where opinions were conflicting, and who possessed anything like the same skill and experience. If there was an opinion, on the one hand, that two years were requisite, and an opinion on the other hand that one year would be sufficient, I would be rather inclined to think that perhaps the truth might be found to lie between; but I would not think there was any reason why I should absolutely accept the one as against the other when presumably each party had sufficient knowledge and experience to form a judgment.

Just one word as to my right hon. friend's reference to my conversion in regard to the possibilities of Canadian manufacture. There has been no conversion on my part; I stated in this House on a great many occasions during last session that I had absolute faith in the manufacturers of Canada to turn out munitions, and I am sure that my right hon. friend, if he will con over the pages of Hansard, will have great difficulty in finding any other opinion expressed by me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think that I should take the trouble.

No, I think you had better not try. As to the tribute which he says I paid to the ex-Minister of Militia and to the work of the committee which he formed, I have heard the ex-Minister of Militia make the same statement in this House as to the wonderful difficulties he experienced in getting manufacturers to go into the manufacture of munitions. I had an opportunity of hearing all those gentlemen in the box under oath within the last eight or nine months.
You can read every statement made by them and you will find no word to show that any man of them had any doubts whatever but, to. use an expression which has been used in this House before-and I do not wish to descend to slang-all I could find was that they fought like blazes *among themselves to see who would get the most contracts. There was no difference between them as to their ability to manufacture and to such an extent did they carry out that idea that- and I am -not now going into, that controversy-it will come up later-when the Shell Committee was put out of office and a new, I believe, better order of things was put in its stead, one or tnese manufacturers whom the ex-minister calls pessimists not only had manufactured some millions of dollars worth of shells for the Shell Committee but he had contracts in his pockets for 100,000 shells which he knew he could not manufacture for a year to come. The first act of the new powers which were placed in control was to cancel that contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Who had the
contract?

I did not say. I said
one firm. You will find it in the evidence taken by the Royal Commission. I will not go into a discussion of that now, but I want to point out that there has been no change of heart on my part. The fact is that instead of each manufacturer being obliged to go into it, every one of them wias simply rushing to get in from the beginning and if there was any difference amongst them it was only to see who would get the biggest contract.

I have listened with
a great deal of interest and I have admired the good nature of the Prime Minister and the way he has endeavoured to answer the questions which have , come from this side. But, there is one phase of the matter that I have not been able to understand thoroughly. We all understand that the Ross rifle has been condemned and that the Lee-Enfield has been adopted. The vital question is to. get the Lee-Enfield and I have not been able to understand why the matter has not been brought to a head by the Government offering Sir Charles Ross an order to make the Lee-Enfield for quick delivery. There should be no mystery about it. He has indicated in his letter that he is able to do it. We want the rifle and instead of speculating and asking people across the water whether it can be done, why not bring it to a head at once by giving an order if he will accept it. Then, we will find out how long it will take him to equip his factory and furnish the Lee-Enfield rifle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are obliged under the terms of the contract, to give a year's notice. Of course, if Sir Charles Ross should be prepared to execute an order within a year it might be done. But my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) will remember that we have to get the actual rifle itself. We were- instructed by the British Government that it would not do to go to the

United States and take five or six of the rifles in process of being manufactured there. They advised, and, indeed, instructed us, that if we proposed to adopt the new British rifle as a standard, the rifles must first be inspected and passed by the chief inspector of small arms in Great Britain. When we attempted, in September last, to expedite the matter by procuring half a dozen of these rifles in the United States	at one
of the factories where they are being produced, we received the telegram which I read this afternoon directing us that these rifles must be first inspected and passed by their chief inspector of small arms, or they could not be recognized as being of the necessary type. The rifles so inspected arrived towards the end of January. That was sufficient for the purpose of directing the Ross Rifle Company to produce a rifle of that type, but it was not sufficient for the purpose of giving an order to the Ross Rifle Company. For that purpose we required the drawings and specifications as well. We asked for these drawings and specifications in September last. We asked for them repeatedly, I think last on the 12th December, but up to the present we have not received them. We cannot give any order in the terms of the contract to the Ross Rifle Company until we do obtain those drawings and specifications; at least I am so advised by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), who has examined the contract with care.

After hearing the opinion of the late Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) this evening as to the great merits of the Ross rifle over the Lee-Enfield, or any other rifle that the world ever heard of, I would think that it would be only frankness on the part of the Prime Minister to say that the ex-Minister of Militia did not encourage haste on the part of the Government in making a change from the Ross rifle to the Lee-Enfield. Apparently it was very difficult for the Government to give a contract foT the Lee-Enfield in Canada while the ex-minister was a member of my right hon. friend's Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend is entirely mistaken about that and this ought to be said in justice to the late Minister of Militia. There is absolutely no doubt about it.
[Sir Robert Borden.3
I am not saying that it was wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to make this clear:	There is absolutely no
douibt about it that he was very confident about the superiority of the Ross rifle over the Lee-Enfield, and I believe he is to-day.

I understood the right hon. gentleman, earlier in the discussion, before dinner, to have mentioned that the notice terminating the contract had been given and the time limited by the notice would expire a year hence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On the first of February, 1918.

Might I inquire whether between now and that time the Ross Company will manufacture solely for the Canadian Government or partly for the Canadian Government and partly for the British Government and if the rifle manufactured will be the Ross rifle?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, they are
manufacturing for both Governments; something over 90,000 for the Canadian Government and nearly 60,000 for the British Government are still undelivered. As I pointed out before recess, we suggested to the British Government-I think in July, 1916, I cannot be sure but the documents

will show-that it might be a wise thing for the two Governments to get into negotiation with the Ross Rifle Company, stop the manufacture of Ross rifles altogether, let the factory be equipped as speedily as possible with the plant necessary to turn out the new type of Lee-Enfield and convert the orders still unfilled of both Governments into orders for the new type of Lee-Enfields.
The British Government made reply, in two different telegrams which I have read to the committee, pointing out that from their standpoint they did not think this advisable; that the Ross rifle was of considerable use to them for certain purposes, and that there would be no difficulty if we saw fit to try to make the change, for the Ross Rifle Company to continue during the process of reorganization to supply the Ross rifle Mark III to the British Government under the contract which had been made in December, 1914.

If I gathered what the
Prime Minister said in answer to a question a few minutes ago, the terms of the contract between the Government and the Ross Rifle 'Company, drawn with a view to the contingency of war arising, did as a matter of fact place the control of the contract in the hands of the Government, and not in the hands of the contractor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not sure
that I caught my hon. friend's point.

The Rose rifle contract,
drawn up with a view to the contingency of war arising, which actually did arise, contained such terms as placed control of the situation in regard to the manufacture of Ross rifles in the hands of the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not
quite agree in that view. I have not the contract before me, and I am speaking subject to correction upon an examination of its terms, but my recollection is that the contract contains the provision that if the Government by reason of war or emergency require a- very largely increased output of rifles in any year, then it shall be the duty of the Government to give notice to the Ross Rifle Company of the number of rifles required, and it shall be the right of the Ross Rifle Company to give notice to the Government that it can not produce more than a certain number of rifles within that period, and then, as to the excess of rifles required, the Government would be at
liberty to obtain them elsewhere. Whether that gives control of the situation or not, that is the fact.

I would certainly say that in effect, if not in letter, it did give the Government control of the situation. In fact, I would say absolute control. In any case it gave the Government absolute control as regards the number of rifles over and above the amount that the Ross Rifle Company could turn out within that period.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they gave us notice.
They, would have to give notice, if the Government gave them notice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They would
have to give us notice if they were unable to do what we required.

Therefore the Government was absolutely free of this contract so far as the number of rifles required by the Government was concerned over and above what the Ross Rifle Company could turn out. Now I do not assume for a moment that it was likely that there need be any friction in the matter at all. I assume that the Ross Rifle Company, being a business organization, would be willing t* meet the Government, just as the Government would be willing to meet them, with a view to making arrangements for meeting the requirements of the country, if the pressure had been exerted in that way. But the evidence we have from the attitude of the ex-Minister of Militia is that so far from pressure being exerted by the Government upon the Ross Rifle Company, the pressure was from the Ross Rifle Company upon the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what way?
In the way that it was the company that dictated the situation, and not the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
The Government accepted the limitations of the Ross Rifle Company, instead of dictating the limitations. Therefore, my contention is that the plea set up in the first place by the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) and later, though not in such definite terms, by the Prime Minister, as the reason why more energetic and effective action was not taken to equip our troops with an efficient rifle, does not hold good; leaving out of consideration altogether the suggestion of the hon. member

for Carleton (Mr. Car veil), that the Government should have exercised dominant rights, which, after all, 13 not such an extra- [DOT] ordinary exercise of power on the part of the Government in case of war. On several occasions, indeed, notably in the commandeering of wheat a year ago, this right has been exercised by the Canadian Government, and also by the British Government, which went to the extent in one case of taking control of the railway transportation of the United. Kingdom. So that there is in fact, as well as in law, no ground for the Government's contention that they were under the dictation of the Ross Rifle Company, instead of the Ross Rifle Company being under their dictation.
I am going to assume that I am one of the plain people, not interested in the Ross Rifle Company, or in the administration of the Government, except in so far as it affects the people of Canada and the win* ning of the war. It is from that standpoint that I do view, and wish to view this question, and with that view I am not able to begin the criticism that I desire to make, at the point where my hon. friend from Carleton started, namely, the summer of 1916, after it had been demonstrated by all the means that could be brought to bear that the Ross rifle was inefficient for the purpose for which it was required. I begin with August 4, 1914. This Government of Canada is equipped, as other governments are for carrying on the responsibilities of government, and among this equipment there is a Department of Militia and Defence, with a minister at its head. It was not a secret that has now developed after two or three years of war, that the rifle is the chief weapon of modern warfare, and that upon its efficiency and the efficiency in its use of the man who uses it rests success or failure. It was the business of the Govt-ernment of Canada, and it was the first business that should have concerned them once war broke out, to see that the rifle in the hands of our troops was efficient. They knew that our men were going up against the most thoroughly trained soldiers in the world, possessing the most efficient equipment that the most scientific nation could provide for the men upon whom it depended in its campaign for world-domination. Under these circumstances, even if there had never been any doubts about the rifle, it was the business of the Government of Canada to take stock of the rifle, at any rate from August 4, and not depend upon
[Mr. Oliver.!
Sir John French or Sir Douglas Haig or any one else across the water to see that our - men had an efficient weapon in their hands. It was the responsibility of Canada to see that that weapon was efficient. As a matter of fact, there had been suspicions in former years against the efficiency of the Ross rifle by the very men who sit on the Government side of the House, so that it cannot be suggested that there was any surprise at the findings of Sir John French or Sir Douglas Haig when those findings at last were made.
If there was one duty that rested upon this Government and upon its Department of Militia more than another it was to follow the troops in the training camp and in the field and be sure that the rifle in their hands was an efficient one. The misfortune of the case appears to be that we had a Minister of Militia who would not and will not believe anything from anybody except that this Ross rifle is the most efficient rifle in the world. The ex-Minister of Militia held that belief and holds it yet, as we have heard here to-night, and the right hon. Premier and his colleagues retained the minister in that responsible position from the beginning until a short time ago. Therefore, the responsibility for the consequences of the failure of the Ross rifle to stand up to the requirements of field service rests absolutely on the heads of the men who lead the Government of to-day. We had no right to wait until Sir John French, on his own responsibility, without the knowledge or consent of this Government, found it necessary, as the result of the terrible experience of the battle of St. Julien, to disarm tine Canadian Division taking part in that battle of Ross rifles and place Lee-Enfield rifles in their hands; and, as he says in words that are graphic, he did so, because he was about to send them into action again. The logic is that his conscience did not permit him to send them again into actipn armed with the Titles that they had when they wrent through the battle of St. Julien.
The ex-Minister of Militia spoke to-night of fain tests or of unfair tests of the Ross rifle. Could there be any test more definite or more final than the fact stated by General French that when he gave the order to rearm the First Division he found three thousand men of that division who had, as he says, without any authority, armed themselves with Lee-Enfield in the place of the Ross rifles. Surely the man on the firing line, the man in the trench, the man whose

life depends upon the efficiency of the weapon in his hands, is a safe judge as to the respective merits of the rifle that his Government has placed in his hands. His natural loyalty to his country would tend to make him keep it if he could have faith in it. Surely, when he (throws that rifle away and picks up the rifle of a dead man lying on the field of battle, there is no further argument or comparison necessary. We do n.ot need to hear from Sir John French or Sir Douglas Haig or any one else: the actions of our own men under stress of circumstance are enough, or should be enough, to settle the question of field efficiency of the Ross rifle. I am at a loss to understand how any set of men charged with the terrible responsibility resting upon the shoulders of the Government of Canada since the 4th. August, 1914, could submit to a continuance of such a condition in regard to the armament of our soldiers until the Army Council of Great Britain issued notice to them not to send over any more Ross rifles, and announced to them that they would arm our troops with Lee-Enfield rifles. A more humiliating position Canada could not be placed in, and how desperate the condition must have been when the Government of Great Britain would insist on doing for our men what our Government would not do for them.
I do not know, and no man can tell how *many Canadian homes have been rendered desolate as the result of the inefficiency of this weapon placed in the hands of our .soldiers by our Government. That was not the immediate concern of (the Imperial Government in insisting upon a change of armament. Their interest in the matter was the success or failure of the military *endeavours being put forward on the battle front; their interest was in the success or failure of the Allied arms. That was the cause that impelled them to insist upon the re-armament Of the Canadian forces with a rifle which our men considered efficient and which they considered efficient.
I cannot agree that even the very lucid and courteous statement made here to-night by the Prime Minister is in any degree an excuse, much less a justification, for the terrible sequence of events of which I have spoken. There must have been some means whereby the application of sufficient directive energy backed by the tremendous capital available from the treasury of Canada, could have put into the hands of our men an efficient weapon from the hands of their -own Government, from their own people.
It w'as possible, so the Prime Minister informed the House last session, to increase , the output of rifles twenty fold in the year and a half that had elapsed since the outbreak of the war. It was possible to create an Enfield rifle factory in the United States; it has been possible to create ammunition factories in many parts of the United States and Canada handling such enormous quantities of munitions of war that the human mind cannot calculate nor grasp the quantity.
It was not possible for the Government of Canada to manufacture, or to secure the manufacture of, sufficient Lee-Enfield rifles to arm the troops of Canada. But it was possible for the Government of Great Britain to do that-for they have done it. To-day, after two and a half years of war, though we had a rifle factory running in good shape in Canada at the beginning of the war, which factory has increased its output twenty times since then-I use the figure given by the Prime Minister-there is not to-day, of all the Canadian forces at the front, one man armed with a Ross rifle, we are informed, and every rifle with which our troops at the front are armed is made and furnished by the British Government. Such a condition is beyond description, it is beyond justification, it is beyond excuse. It can only be ascribed to the fact that we have had a Minister of Militia who, in the case of the Ross rifle, as in case of other militia equipment, has insisted on his own views as against the views of those who are in control of the army of Great Britain.
Now, I should be the last to admit superiority in ability on the part of any other people over the people of Canada. I should be glad to back the Minister of Militia or any other member of the Government-perhaps I might except the exMinister of Militia-but I would be willing to back the members of the Government generally-against an equal number of men of equal rank in any other country. But it is not a question of the respective abilities of the men in control of our affairs and those in control of affairs in Great Britain. The men in control of affairs in Great Britain are the people who are running the thing; it is their say; and if we are going to_ help to win the war, we must do it by helping them and not by going counter to their ideas. When it pleases them to require a rifle of a certain style, or equipment of a certain style, it is for us to provide that which will conform with their idea, so that we may work with

them harmoniously. We may think that we have as good as they have or better; but so long as they are carrying the big end of the burden, if we are going to be successful in helping them we must co-operate with them and not antagonize them by the equipment, munitions, or armament we bring forward.
This matter is very much more than a question of a contract between our Government and the Ross Rifle Company. It is a matter which, in the eyes of the British Government, was of such a character and of such importance that the winning of the war depended upon that Government taking the matter into their own hands. But if it was important to the British Government in the winning of the war, it was just as important to the people of Canada in the winning of the war. And it was a thousand times more important to the people of Canada in the preservation of the lives and limbs of the men whom they sent to fight the battles of Canada, the Empire and the world. These men came forward and gave themselves freely for the cause, leaving home, and friends, and property, and business, and prospects, to fight for an ideal, to fight for their country, for its honour and its safety; and we place in their hands a weapon upon which they cannot depend, in which they have lost confidence, which means that they have been slaughtered by our enemies because we did not do our duty by them by giving to them the weapon that they should have had to put them on equal terms with our enemies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I regret that
my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) should have made the extraordinary and extravagant statements which have just fallen from his lips. He apparently put out of sight and consideration the fact that those responsible for the administration of public affairs have been as anxious as he or any one else in this country could be to see to it that the men whom Canada has sent to the front were supplied with as good a weapon as possible. Does he realize that he is making this attack upon a weapon for which he himself is responsible? Does he realize that he sat on the Treasury benches, a _ member of the late Administration in 1908, when serious question arose about this rifle and that his colleague in the Government, speaking words for which he, as a member of the .Government, was responsible, took the ground that this was the best rifle that

.Canada could secure? I wonder if he realizes this, when he makes the most extraordinary statements that have fallen from ibis lips this evening. The words which I .have under my hand are his words, because they were uttered by one of his colleagues in the Government. Why, he even took the ground, through one of his colleagues, that-
The Ross rifle, in common with all other rifles, military or sporting, may he said to have certain defects, structural weaknesses, or deficiencies. It is not the custom of any government to publish to the world what it considers the weak points of the arms with which its troops are equipped.
This was an absolute denial that the Commons of Canada, the representatives of the people, should be given any knowledge of what the alleged deficiencies of this rifle were. He is responsible also for the statement that this rifle had been bent to the War Office and had been tested, and had been carefully reported upon, and was a good rifle. He is responsible for many other statements which I have under my hand but which I will not take time to quote to-night. I should like to have him understand that when this war broke out in 1914 the military forces of Canada were equipped with a rifle which had been deliberately selected by the hon. gentleman himself. He says that some further test should then have been made. I should like to ask any member of this House, or any other honourable and reasonable man in this country, how, with these statements and many more from hon. gentlemen on.the other side of the House, it would be possible to test that rifle further except by active service in the field. Will my hon. friend tell me how? Does he know of any means by which, it could foe tested other than by actual practical experience in the field? 1 do not know of any

My complaint is that when it- was tested by actual service in the field -which did not happen when the Liberal Government was responsible-my hon. friends did not take notice of the results of those tests.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I deny absolutely the assertion which the hon. gentleman has made. We did take notice of it, and we acquiesced at once in the determination of the military authorities at the front that the first division should be armed with Lee-Enfields, and that the Ross rifle should be put aside for the time being. It then became the duty of the Government to do

what best could he done; we had to consider. what was the best course that lay before us. I have already pointed out that the urgent question then was whether any rifle whatever could be obtained for arming the British and Allied troops about to go to the front. That question was so "urgent that the British Government were willing to accept, if they could obtain them, rifles of a very antiquated type, and they asked us to co-operate with them for the purpose of obtaining them. The apparent difficulty with the rifle then was the jamming caused by ammunition which was not fitted for the rifle, being somewhat larger than that produced in Canada. The only remedy to be applied, so far as we understood-, was to enlarge the chamber of the rifle. My hon. friend himself had taken the responsibility, which rests on him heavily to-day if he has a conscience, of fixing a chamber of .460 for a cartridge of precisely the same calibre. As I pointed out, a little bit of dirt or anything that would adhere to the cartridge would inevitably cause jamming. That was the condition which my hon. friend had created, with the advice of hi-s experts, with regard to the rifle which he put in the hands of the Canadian troops. We were told some time ago that the boots provided by the late Government were never intended for war, but only for peace. Are we to understand that the rifle which my hon. friend put into the hands of the Canadian troops was intended only for peace, not for war? Is that the position which he takes before this committee and before the people? If our troops were not to go without rifles, there was only one thing to do, and that was to enlarge. the chamber of the rifle so that the cartridges would be less liable to jam than if the chamber were left as it was. In that regard we took exactly the same course that the British Government took with regard to the Lee-Enfield rifle. They enlarged the chamber; we enlarged our chamber. We proposed- at first to enlarge it from .460 to .462; we eventually enlarged it to .464. After the chamber had been enlarged, tests were made, and it was thought that the rifle would- be serviceable under these new conditions. The course which we took had been suggested in the report of Sir John Frehch himself, and we carried it out with reasonable belief that it would make the rifle a serviceable one. We had as good reason to come to that conclusion as the British Government had to reach the conclusion that the enlargement of the chamber of the Lee-Enfield rifle would be
attended with a like result. When my hon. friend casts these sneers at us and makes these absurd reproaches against the Government, he does not do himself credit. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are as conscientious and inspired with as full a sense of duty towards the people of this country as he ever was or ever will be. It comes ill from my hon. friend, having regard to some of his own administrative experiences, to cast reproaches of this character upon men who are inspired by no desire in this war except that of doing their full duty to the people of Canada and to the men at the front. He has made absurd suggestions-well, I will withdraw that word, it is -unparliamentary

he has made suggestions which seem to me very unreasonable. He has suggested that the Ross Rifle Company was dictating to the Government. I take issue with him absolutely. The Ross Rifle Company never attempted to dictate to the Government; if they had attempted to do so, the Government would not have submitted to their dictation. The hon. gentleman misinterpreted my remarks with regard to expropriation. I did not suggest that the Government might not in a proper case expropriate or that they would have consideration for the wishes of the Ross Rifle Company if they thought that expropriation were proper and in the best interests'of the people. If the Government expropriated the property, compensation would be made to the Ross Rifle Company, who would have no cause of complaint nor do I believe that they would have made any complaint. The question- was whether the Government, if they took over the Ross Rifle factory, could operate it more efficiently than it was being operated by the company itself. I am bound to tell my hon. friend that I am absolutely -unable to follow his reasoning or to understand what he means when he arrives at the curious argumentative conclusion that upon the terms of the contract as they have been placed upon Hansard we -had control of the situation in case war should break out or emergency arise. I do-ufot very much whether he himself understands what he mean-s. How could we have control of the situation? If the Ross Rifle Company were called upon to produce a number of rifles which they were unable to turn out in a given period, they could give us notice and we could go elsewhere. * How did that give us any control of the situation, when- the (British" Government

were raking the four corners of the earth trying to get rifles and failing to get them? What advantage would it be to ns if the company should give u3 notice that they could not turn out rifles when we could not get them anywhere else? My hon. friend finds fault with us because we retained the Minister of Militia, who had confidence in the Ross rifle. Surely my hon. friend does not suggest that before the Ross rifle has been pronounced unsuitable toy the military authorities at the front, we should have discarded it? What reason would we have for discarding it before actual experience at the front had shown, in the estimation of the military authorities, that it was unsuitable? And when they did pronounce it to toe unsuitable, the Minister of Militia and Defence, as I have already declared to the committee, interposed no objection to the course which was taken; he assented at once to the proposed action of the military authorities, both in 1915 and in 1916. When my hon. friend, for some reason unknown to me, suggests this rifle should have been discarded on the outbreak of the war, does he realize that the British Government in the month of December, 1914, ordered
100,000	of these same Ross rifles? That seemed to me to afford fairly reasonable evidence fhat the rifle was a service-, able rifle; otherwise, for what reason would the British Government have given a large order of that kind, costing $2,500,000 or $3,000,000? We can hardly suppose that they felt themselves to be endowed with such astonishing resources that they could throw to the winds $2,500,000 or $3,000,000 for a rifle which they did not believe to be serviceable. As I said before, the rifle had been approved by the late Government in the form in which we found it when war broke out. The Minister of Militia believed it to be a good rifle. We had no evidence before us that it was not a good rifle until experience in actual warfare, under conditions of the utmost severity, demonstrated, in the opinion of the military authorities at the front, that it ought to be put aside and the Lee-Enfield substituted for it. They made that suggestion to us, and we acquiesced in it. When later on, in the summer of 1916, they made the further suggestion that all Canadian troops at the front should be armed with the Lee-Enfield, instead of the Ross rifle, we again acquiesced. Tnat is the whole situation, and I repeat once more that, in my opinion, it affords no ground whatever for the violent reproaches which 	-
my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has seen fit to
level against the Government in this connection.
Mr. OLIVER; I will not delay the House at any great length, and I do not intend to follow the Prime Minister in everything he has said. But his suggestion as to my responsibility for the Ross rifle is really hardly to the point. I was a member of the Government which instituted the making of the Ross rifle, and I have nothing to apologize for in regard to that matter. The contract has been read here to-night. It was a good contract, and the rifle was a good rifle for target and sporting purposes, or for any purpose for which it was used up to the outbreak of war. The Prrme Minister adopts the very cheap suggestion that it was a rifle for peace, and not for war; it was a rifle which had been used in peace until the outbreak of war. That was the only use there was for it, and it was found to be absolutely satisfactory, to be not only as good as others, but better than others. There is, therefore, no apology necessary from any member of the Liberal Government which made this contract for the Ross rifle as it was when war broke out. But once wax broke out, this Government, and not the late Government, became responsible, and when under war conditions the Ross rifle was found to be not satisfactory, when it was found that the troops using it could not depend upon it, when
3,000	of them threw it away and took Lee-Enfields because they believed that their lives depended on making the change, the responsibility for retaining that rifle was the responsibility of this Government and not of the late Liberal Government. I do not share the responsibility for the retention of the Ross rifles by our troops. My hon. friend spoke of my conscience. I am . trying to rid my soul of the blood of the men who died in France because we, the people of Canada, armed them with an inferior weapon. As to the provsion in the contract, which my right hon. friend says he does not understand, and that I do not understand-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that I did not understand.
Then that I did not understand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that.

Then I beg the Prime
Minister's pardon; I accept his correction.

I would ask him for what purpose can it be imagined that that provision was placed in the contract except to exactly meet such a condition as arose on the outbreak of war, so as to place the Government of the country in a position to provide such rifles as they wished, and as many as they needed for the arming of their troops. There could be no other reason for placing that provision in the contract. That is why I believe the provision was well framed to achieve the purpose that I mention.
To repeat, on this point, the Prime Minister seemed to think that I found fault with the Government because they had taken the rifle to the battlefield. I did not find fauilt with the Government'for that. I do not expect this Government, or any other Government, to be omniscient, to see or know things that have not yet occurred. I absolutely relieve the Government from any responsibility for taking the rifle to the battlefield, and placing it in the hands of the troops for service in France. They had every reason, or at all events, some reason to believe that the rifle was a good rifle; but, as I have already stated, the rifle was under suspicion by the very men who sat around the Prime Minister, and whether it was under suspicion or not, the exigencies of the case were such that it was the business of the Government of Canada to follow events on the battlefield so that on their responsibility, and not on that of British officers, they would be sure that our men had, or had not, in their hands a rifle that was absolutely efficient. I absolutely protest against the responsibility being placed on any other shoulders than those of our own military department, who are charged on our behalf with seeing that our troops are efficient, and that their armament is efficient. It is not the responsibility of the British Government; it is the responsibility of our Government. After experience had shown that the rifle was inefficient, not on the authority of Sir John French, but on the experience of our own men who threw it away, there was no escape from the responsibility of the Government to see that that rifle was replaced as soon as it could be. The Prime Minister has suggested that the Government did everything they could to meet the situation. I recall that on the 17th May last, when the question of the efficiency of the Ross rifle was under consideration in this House, his colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Rogers) suggested, if he did not absolutely make the threat, that he would
imprison any man who questioned the efficiency of the Ross rifle. He stated from his place in the House that on the information which he had, he had no reason to believe other than that the Ross rifle was an absolutely efficient rifle; and yet in the hands of the Prime Minister at that time, on that very day, and for five days previously, there had been a cablegram from the accredited agent of the Militia Department in London saying, "Serious condition has arisen regarding Ross rifle. Show this to the Prime Minister." I do not wish to make this the occasion of an exchange of compliments, but as the Prime Minister has been handing a few bouquets to me, I take the opportunity of handing this to him for his consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am very much obliged to my hon. friend. His bouquets are so frequent and so fragrant that they are always welcome. I do not desire to repeat what I have already said about ten times since three okdock this afternoon, but which does not yet seem to have reached the inner consciousness of my hon. friend: that when the military authorities at the front, whom we considered the 'best judges, directed arming of the Canadian troops with the Lee-Enfield rifle, we acquiesced in it. I leave the situation there, but with this further statement: that we then made the best arrangement we found -possible, and which we conceived to be a reasonable arrangement, for improving the Ross rifle so that the jamming, the only defect which had' been seriously urged against it up to that time, would be remedied. Again in 1916, we took a like course and in taking it we had the engagement of the British Government that all our troops at the front would be armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle If that does not satisfy my hon. friend as to our desire and intention to do our duty in the matter, if it does not satisfy him that we did our reasonable duty in the matter to the best of our ability, or to the best of the ability of any Government that might have been called upon to deal with the situation, why, he and I shall have to be content to differ about the matter. I should say to him with all courtesy and all respect that all that he has urged in so strong, and even so violent, a manner has not in the least disturbed my opinion as to the wisdom of the course which we took. I do not see that we could have taken any other course, nor do I see that any other course would have been open to any government. It is impossible to complete the discussion this



evening; indeed, I made an engagement with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that the committee should sit on a subsequent day, and I therefore beg to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Will the Prime Minister bear in mind the request which I made to look up in the department-

In regard to
bolts?

Yes, and also the applications made to the company for changes, when they were made, and when they were complied with, if any were complied with.
